text: [[fossil|Fossil]] poo is called a [[coprolite|coprolite]]. It's poo that turned to stone.
Coprolites show what ancient animals ate, which is hard to learn any other way. Inside them, scientists find crushed bones, bits of plants, seeds, fish scales and even tiny [[parasite|parasites]].

In 2005, coprolites from Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh showed that dinosaurs ate grass. That changed the history of grass. A giant T. rex coprolite from Canada is full of crushed bone, proof of its bone-crunching bite.

frames.cap: A giant sauropod munches plants in central India, about 67 million years ago.
It leaves a dropping. Most poo rots away. But this one gets buried quickly in mud.
Over millions of years, minerals turn it into stone. Now it's a coprolite, and it doesn't smell!
Under a microscope, scientists found tiny silica pieces made by grass plants inside.
Surprise! Grass already existed in the dinosaur age. Scientists used to think it came much later.

options.t: Minerals have replaced it, so it is now stone
Dinosaur poo never smelled in the first place

quiz.reveal: Over millions of years, water carrying minerals soaked into the buried dung and slowly turned it to rock. The smelly chemicals are long gone. What is left is a stone with the shape, and sometimes the contents, of the original poo.

sec.t:
The first person to notice fossil poo was probably [[@mary-anning|Mary Anning]], the fossil hunter of Lyme Regis in England. She found strange stones inside the skeletons of ichthyosaurs, where their stomachs would have been. When broken open, the stones held fish bones and scales.

In 1829, the [[geologist|geologist]] William Buckland studied them and gave them their name, coprolite, from Greek words for "dung" and "stone". Buckland was famous for being eccentric. He even had a table made with polished coprolites set into its top.

For a long time, scientists believed grass had appeared after the dinosaurs died out. Then, in 2005, a team led by the Indian scientist Vandana Prasad studied coprolites from Pisdura in Maharashtra. They had probably been left by titanosaurs, about 67 million years ago.

Inside were tiny pieces of silica called phytoliths. Grasses make them in their leaves, and each kind of plant makes its own shapes. Some of the phytoliths came from grasses. So grass existed in India while dinosaurs were alive, and the giants were eating it.

In 2011, the same team reported phytoliths from plants related to [[@rice|rice]] in these coprolites. That pushed the history of the rice family back too. The dinosaurs ate a wide mix, including conifers, palms and other plants.

In 1998, the American scientist Karen Chin described a coprolite found in Saskatchewan, Canada. It was about 44 cm long, longer than a school ruler and a half, and much of it was crushed bone. Only one meat-eater big enough lived there at the time: T. rex.

The bone fragments showed that T. rex did not just tear flesh. It crunched through bone and swallowed it, something few animals can do. It is strong evidence for the [[@trex-bite|powerful bite]] that its skull and teeth also suggest.

Chin has also studied coprolites from plant-eating dinosaurs in Montana and Utah. Many were full of rotting wood, and some from Utah held bits of crab or crayfish shell. The dinosaurs may have eaten rotting logs at certain times of year, perhaps for the [[fungus|fungi]] and small animals living inside them. Like a detective with a [[@magnifying-glass|magnifying glass]], a scientist with a slice of coprolite can find a dinosaur's last meal.

sec.t:
कीचड़ और रेत से बनने वाली चट्टान परत-दर-परत जमती है, एक के ऊपर एक, जैसे रोज़ के अख़बारों का बढ़ता ढेर। 1669 में डेनमार्क के वैज्ञानिक निकोलस स्टेनो ने इसके पीछे का सीधा नियम लिखा। अगर किसी चीज़ ने परतों को उलट-पुलट न दिया हो, तो सबसे नीचे की परतें सबसे पुरानी होती हैं और सबसे ऊपर की सबसे नई।

हर परत यह भी दर्ज करती है कि वह कैसे बनी। जिस रेत के अंदर तिरछी लकीरें हों, वह अक्सर रेगिस्तान के टीलों से आती है। फटी हुई मिट्टी का मतलब है कि कोई पोखर धूप में सूखा था। गोल कंकड़ों का मतलब है तेज़ बहती नदी। [[@grand-canyon|ग्रैंड कैन्यन]] की दीवारें बदलती दुनियाओं की ऐसी ही परत पर परत दिखाती हैं, उथले समुद्रों से लेकर रेतीले रेगिस्तानों तक।

पौधे मौसम दर्ज करने में माहिर हैं। गरम, नम जगहों पर बहुत-से पेड़ों की पत्तियों के किनारे चिकने होते हैं। ठंडी जगहों पर ज़्यादा पेड़ों की पत्तियों के किनारे कटे-फटे, दाँतेदार होते हैं। अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक जैक वुल्फ़ ने इसी पैटर्न से सिर्फ़ जीवाश्म पत्तियों के सहारे प्राचीन जंगलों का तापमान निकाला।

[[@antarctica|अंटार्कटिका]] में कोयला और ग्लोसोप्टेरिस नाम के पौधे की जीवाश्म पत्तियाँ मिलती हैं। भारत में भी। यह उन सुरागों में से एक है जो बताते हैं कि दोनों कभी जुड़े थे, और [[@india-drift|भारत खिसकते हुए]] धरती के आर-पार आया। कोयला खुद दबे-कुचले प्राचीन पौधे हैं, जैसा तुम [[@oil-coal|कोयला और तेल कैसे बने]] में पढ़ सकते हो।

तमिलनाडु में [[@puducherry|पुदुच्चेरी]] के पास पेड़ों के गिरे हुए तने पड़े हैं, जो पूरी तरह पत्थर बन चुके हैं। लाखों सालों में [[@groundwater|ज़मीन के नीचे के पानी]] में घुले खनिजों ने लकड़ी की जगह ले ली, कोशिका-दर-कोशिका, और छल्लों और छाल का आकार ज्यों का त्यों रहा। भारतीय भूवैज्ञानिक सर्वेक्षण इन्हें तिरुवक्करई के राष्ट्रीय जीवाश्म काष्ठ उद्यान में सँभालता है। ये दिखाते हैं कि जहाँ आज खेत हैं, वहाँ कभी एक विशाल जंगल खड़ा था।

sec.h: बर्फ़ और मिट्टी, जो याद रखती हैं
sec.t:
कुछ डायरियाँ बर्फ़ में लिखी होती हैं। अंटार्कटिका में लाखों सालों से बर्फ़ गिरती और दबकर परतें बनाती रही है। वैज्ञानिक इसमें से लंबे बेलन खोदकर निकालते हैं, जिन्हें आइस कोर कहते हैं। इनके अंदर फँसे नन्हे बुलबुलों में प्राचीन हवा के असली नमूने होते हैं। अब तक पढ़ा गया सबसे लंबा रिकॉर्ड लगभग 8 लाख साल पीछे जाता है और [[@ice-ages|हिमयुगों]] को आते-जाते दिखाता है। 2025 में यूरोप की एक टीम ने 12 लाख साल से भी पुरानी बर्फ़ खोदकर निकाली, जिसका वैज्ञानिक अब अध्ययन कर रहे हैं।

झीलों की मिट्टी भी रिकॉर्ड रखती है। हर साल [[pollen|पराग]] के कण तली में बैठ जाते हैं, जो बताते हैं कि आस-पास कौन-से पौधे उगते थे। [[@sahara|सहारा]] की पुरानी झीलों की तली की मिट्टी घास और पेड़ों के पराग से भरी है। वहाँ की प्राचीन चट्टानों पर बने चित्रों में जिराफ़, मवेशी और तैराक दिखते हैं, उस जगह पर जो आज रेत है।

text: Yes, ice can be hot, though not anywhere on Earth's surface. The ice in your freezer is just one kind. Scientists know of about 20 different kinds of solid water ice. Each one has its [[molecule|molecules]] packed in a different pattern.

Most of them need huge [[pressure|pressure]]. If you squeeze water hard enough, its molecules are pushed into tight crystals that stay solid even when they are very hot. One type, ice VII, can be solid at hundreds of degrees. Another, superionic ice, was made in a lab in 2019 at thousands of degrees, hotter than the surface of a [[lava|lava]] flow. It may fill the insides of giant planets.

st.reveal: Squeeze water hard enough and its molecules are pushed into a tight crystal that can't easily break apart, even when hot. At pressures tens of thousands of times greater than our air, ice can be hotter than a kitchen oven and still be solid.

sec.h: Why ordinary ice is the odd one
sec.t:
The ice we know, called ice Ih by scientists, is strange. Its molecules hold hands in open six-sided rings with lots of empty space. That makes it lighter than liquid water, which is why [[@why-ice-floats|ice floats]]. Most solids sink in their own liquid.

That open pattern is easy to crush. Press harder and the rings collapse into denser shapes. Scientists have named the different ices with Roman numerals, from ice I up to ice XIX and beyond, in the order they were found. Some of these ices exist only in labs. Others probably form naturally deep inside big icy moons such as Jupiter's Ganymede, where the weight of ice and water above squeezes the lower layers into denser kinds.

Ice VII is not just a lab trick. In 2018, scientists studying [[@made-diamonds|diamonds]] from deep in the Earth found tiny pockets of ice VII trapped inside them. The diamonds had formed hundreds of kilometres down, where water was squeezed into this dense ice.

The diamond acted like a pressure-proof safe. It held the ice tight even after the stone reached the surface. This was the first time ice VII had been found in nature, and it showed that there is water deep in Earth's [[mantle|mantle]].

Superionic ice is stranger still. In 2019, scientists from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California fired a powerful laser in New York at a thin layer of water. For a few billionths of a second, it reached pressures millions of times higher than our air and temperatures of thousands of degrees.

In that state, the oxygen [[atom|atoms]] lock into a solid frame, but the hydrogen bits flow through it like a liquid. It is part solid, part flowing, and black rather than clear. Because charged hydrogen moves through it, it carries electricity.

[[@uranus-sideways|Uranus]] and Neptune are sometimes called "ice giants". Deep inside, scientists think, water may be squeezed into superionic ice. That could explain their wonky magnetic fields, which tilt away from their spin in odd directions.

Some planets around other stars may be mostly water too. Gliese 436 b, a planet about 30 light years away, is hot enough to boil water at our pressures, yet some scientists suggested it might hold hot, squeezed ice deep inside. And the strangest part? The closest planet to the Sun, [[@mercury-planet|Mercury]], has ordinary cold ice hidden in the shadows of its [[crater|craters]].

text: Starlings fly in giant flocks, called murmurations, by following simple rules. Each bird keeps an eye on about six or seven of its closest neighbours. It matches their speed and direction, stays close, but not too close. When one bird turns, its neighbours turn, and the change ripples across the flock in a split second.

There's no leader. Yet the whole flock can twist, split and come back together like a single shape-shifting cloud. Scientists think murmurations help protect the birds from falcons and hawks, and help them gather before roosting for the night.

st.prompt: How many neighbours does each starling in a murmuration pay attention to?

options.t: Just one, the bird in front

st.reveal: Scientists in Rome filmed flocks with several cameras and rebuilt them in 3D. Each bird reacted to about six or seven nearby birds, whether they were close or far apart. That's enough to pass a change across the whole flock in a moment.

src: Ballerini, M. et al. (2008), Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
RSPB (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds), Starling murmurations.

src.Reynolds, C. (1987), Flocks, herds and s: a distributed behavioral model, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH).

n.certNote: Scientists have measured how starlings follow their neighbours, and how flocks move. They still debate exactly why murmurations happen, though protection from predators is the leading idea.

myth: A flock of starlings follows a leader bird.
There's no leader. Each bird just reacts to a handful of its neighbours. A turn can start anywhere, and ripple through the whole flock faster than any single bird could signal it.

sec.t:
Murmurations happen mostly on autumn and winter evenings, just before sunset. Starlings fly in from the fields where they've been feeding all day and gather above a roost, such as a reedbed, a woodland or even a pier.

A flock might have a few thousand birds, or hundreds of thousands. Some have been estimated at more than a million. In Rome, enormous flocks swirl over the city in winter, and in parts of Britain, crowds gather just to watch.

India gets its own show. Each winter, rosy starlings arrive from Central Asia, and their flocks swirl over fields and [[wetland|wetlands]] in states like Rajasthan and Gujarat.

When a starling at the edge spots danger, it swerves. Its neighbours copy it, and their neighbours copy them. That wave of turning can sweep across a flock of hundreds of birds in about half a second.

Scientists found that a change in direction travels through a starling flock almost without fading, as if the flock were one big body. It's a bit like a Mexican wave in a cricket stadium, only in three dimensions and much faster.

The most popular explanation is safety. A [[@sky-peregrine|peregrine falcon]] hunting a starling needs to pick out one bird. In a swirling crowd, that's very hard. The more birds, the less chance any one of them gets caught.

Murmurations may also help birds stay warm together at night, swap information about good feeding places, or simply call more starlings to the roost. Scientists still debate how much each reason matters.

In 1986, an American computer scientist, Craig Reynolds, made a program called "Boids". Each pretend bird followed three simple rules: avoid bumping, match your neighbours' direction, and stay close to the group.

On screen, they flocked just like real birds. The same idea was used for the swarms of bats in the 1992 film *Batman Returns*, and is now used for crowds and herds in films and video games. It shows how simple [[@algorithms|algorithms]], followed by many individuals, can create complex [[@patterns-nature|patterns in nature]].

Starlings aren't native to North America. In 1890, a man named Eugene Schieffelin released about 60 starlings in New York's Central Park, and more the next year. Today there are tens of millions across the continent.

Some say he wanted every bird mentioned by Shakespeare to live in America, but historians have found little proof of that story. What's certain is that starlings spread fast. Their flocks follow rules that other animals share too, from fish swimming in schools to [[@ants-world|ants]] working together without a boss.

text: The smallest animal with a backbone is a frog. The Brazilian flea toad, found in the forests of north-east Brazil, has males about 7 mm long. A whole adult frog could sit on your little fingernail with space left over.

Without a backbone, animals get smaller still. Fairyflies are wasps so tiny that some could pass through the eye of a needle. The male of one [[species|species]] is about 0.14 mm long, smaller than a full stop on this page. Every one of these creatures has a brain, muscles, a gut and a way to have babies, all packed into a speck.

sec.t:
In 2012, scientists in Papua New Guinea found a frog about 7.7 mm long and crowned it the smallest [[vertebrate|vertebrate]]. Then in 2024, careful measurements of the Brazilian flea toad, described in 2011, came in even smaller.

India has miniature frogs too. In 2017, researchers described several new night frogs from the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], some about 12 mm long, small enough to sit on a thumbnail. They had been missed for years because their calls sounded like insects.

Some of the smallest fish, from the peat swamps of Sumatra, are under 1 cm long when fully grown.

The bee hummingbird lives only in Cuba. It is about 5 to 6 cm long, including the beak, and weighs about 2 grams. That is less than a one-rupee coin. Its nest is the size of a bottle cap and its eggs are as small as coffee beans.

For [[mammal|mammals]], there are two winners. The Etruscan shrew, found from Europe to South and Southeast Asia, weighs about 2 grams. The bumblebee bat of Thailand and Myanmar has a body about 3 cm long, and its wings stretch only about 17 cm from tip to tip. Both must eat almost all the time, because small bodies lose heat very fast.

The Etruscan shrew's heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute, and it may eat close to twice its own weight in insects every day. If a ten-year-old ate like that, they would need to munch through dozens of kilograms of food between breakfast and bedtime.

{{story:hummingbirds}}

In 2021, scientists described *Brookesia nana*, a chameleon from northern [[@madagascar|Madagascar]]. The male's body is about 13.5 mm long, and about 22 mm with its tail. It could balance on the tip of your finger.

It lives in leaf litter on the forest floor and climbs low stems at night to sleep. Unlike [[@power-chameleon|larger chameleons]], it is a dull brown and doesn't put on colourful displays.

Fairyflies lay their eggs inside the eggs of other insects. Their [[larva|larvae]] grow up in that tiny space. To save room, one kind has nerve cells that lose their [[nucleus|nucleus]], the cell's control centre, as the wasp grows up. Their wings are thin stalks fringed with hairs, like feathers.

At that size, air feels thick, a bit like honey does to us. The hairs let them "row" through it.

Smaller still are myxozoans, [[parasite|parasites]] distantly related to jellyfish. Some are made of just a few cells and are invisible without a [[@microscopes|microscope]].

Being tiny lets an animal live in places others can't: inside an egg, between leaves, in a crack of bark. Small animals need little food overall, though they eat a lot for their size.

But small has limits. A body can only shrink so far before there is no room for a heart, eyes and eggs. Shrews and hummingbirds sit near that edge, burning energy so fast that a few hours without food can kill them. The flip side of tiny is mighty: some of the smallest creatures are also the [[@extreme-strongest-animals|strongest for their size]].

गर्दन अपने आप में एक अजूबा है। तुम्हारी तरह जिराफ़ की गर्दन में भी बस सात हड्डियाँ होती हैं। बस हर एक बहुत बड़ी होती है, लगभग 25 सेंटीमीटर तक लंबी।

तुम्हारा दिल हर धड़कन में [[@blood|खून]] को दबाव की लगभग 120 इकाइयों से धकेलता है। डॉक्टर इसे मिलीमीटर ऑफ़ मरकरी नाम के पैमाने पर नापते हैं। जिराफ़ का दिल इसका लगभग दोगुना दबाव लगाता है। इस अतिरिक्त दबाव का बड़ा हिस्सा बस [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] के ख़िलाफ़ लंबी गर्दन में खून ऊपर उठाने में खप जाता है।

हिसाब यह रहा। 2 मीटर ऊँचा खून का खंभा लगभग 150 इकाइयों के बराबर नीचे की ओर दबाता है। इसलिए दिल को कम से कम इतने ज़ोर से धकेलना ही पड़ेगा कि खून दिमाग की ऊँचाई तक पहुँचे, और फिर उसे बहता रखने के लिए थोड़ा और।

जिराफ़ के दिल के बाएँ हिस्से की दीवारें मोटी और मज़बूत होती हैं। 2016 में जिराफ़ के [[gene|जीन]] पढ़ने वाले वैज्ञानिकों को कई ऐसे बदलाव मिले जो दिल की बढ़त और रक्तचाप से जुड़े हैं।

ऊँचे दबाव से दूसरे सिरे पर एक नई मुश्किल खड़ी होती है। टाँगों का खून दिल से बहुत नीचे होता है, और गुरुत्वाकर्षण वहाँ दबाव और बढ़ा देता है। किसी इंसान में इससे खून की नलियों से तरल रिसने लगेगा, और टखने गुब्बारों की तरह सूज जाएँगे।

जिराफ़ सूजते नहीं। उनकी टाँगों की त्वचा बहुत कसी और मोटी होती है, और नीचे एक सख़्त परत होती है, जो नलियों को कसे मोज़ों की तरह दबाए रखती है। उनकी टाँगों की [[artery|धमनियों]] की दीवारें भी मोटी होती हैं।

1980 और 1990 के दशक में नासा के वैज्ञानिक एलन हार्गेन्स ने ठीक इसी वजह से जिराफ़ों का अध्ययन किया। [[@spacesuits|स्पेस सूट]] पहने और कम गुरुत्वाकर्षण में रहने वाले अंतरिक्ष यात्रियों के शरीर में तरल इधर-उधर खिसकने लगता है, जिससे दिक़्क़त होती है। जिराफ़ों ने इसे अपनी जगह टिकाए रखने का एक कुदरती तरीका दिखाया।

{{story:heart-beat}}

जिराफ़ के सिर के लिए सबसे ख़तरनाक पल वह होता है जब वह पानी पीने के लिए झुकता है। उसका सिर दिल से 2 मीटर ऊपर से झूलकर उससे एक मीटर से भी ज़्यादा नीचे आ जाता है। खून को तो नीचे दौड़कर दिमाग में भर जाना चाहिए।

पर ऐसा नहीं होता, कई तरकीबों की बदौलत। गर्दन की बड़ी [[vein|नसों]] के अंदर के वाल्व खून को उल्टा बहने से रोकते हैं। गर्दन की लचीली धमनियाँ गुब्बारे की तरह झटकों को सोख लेती हैं। वैज्ञानिक यह भी मानते हैं कि दिमाग के निचले हिस्से के पास छोटी नलियों का एक जाल दबाव के उतार-चढ़ाव को हल्का करता है, हालाँकि यह कितना काम करता है, इस पर वे अब भी बहस करते हैं।

पानी तक पहुँचने के लिए जिराफ़ अपनी अगली टाँगें खूब फैला देते हैं। इस हालत में वे बेढंगे हो जाते हैं और खड़े होने में देर लगाते हैं, इसलिए जल्दी-जल्दी पीते हैं और बार-बार चारों ओर शेरों के लिए नज़र दौड़ाते हैं।

जिराफ़ अफ़्रीका के सूखे घास के मैदानों और खुले जंगलों में रहते हैं, पश्चिम में नाइजर और चाड से लेकर केन्या और तंज़ानिया तक, और नीचे दक्षिण अफ़्रीका तक। ऊँचाई की वजह से वे बबूल के पेड़ों की चोटियों से पत्तियाँ चर लेते हैं। इसके लिए वे लगभग 45 सेंटीमीटर लंबी गहरे रंग की जीभ टहनियों पर लपेट लेते हैं।

वे ज़्यादा नहीं सोते, अक्सर दिन में बस कुछ घंटे, छोटे-छोटे टुकड़ों में, कभी-कभी खड़े-खड़े ही। नर जिराफ़ "नेकिंग" नाम की लड़ाइयों में अपनी गर्दन हथौड़े की तरह घुमाते हैं। एक लंबा नर लगभग 5.5 मीटर तक पहुँच सकता है, यानी किसी कार के ऊपर डबल-डेकर बस खड़ी कर दो, उतना ऊँचा।

जंगल में जिराफ़ देखने हों, तो [[@kenya-safari|केन्या की सफ़ारी]] पर जाओ। और सबसे अजीब बात? कुछ डायनासोरों की गर्दनें जिराफ़ से कई गुना लंबी थीं, और वैज्ञानिक अब भी बहस करते हैं कि वे अपने सिर तक खून कैसे पहुँचाते थे। इसके बारे में [[@sauropod-necks|सॉरोपॉड की लंबी गर्दनें]] में पढ़ो।

text: Light enters your eye and lands on the [[retina|retina]] at the back, where millions of light-sensing cells live.

Three kinds of cone cells respond to different colours of light. One kind reacts most to reddish light, one to green and one to blue. Your brain compares how strongly each kind is firing. A ripe mango might set off the red and green cones strongly and the blue ones hardly at all, and your brain reads that mix as orange-yellow.
That's also why screens can fool you with just red, green and blue dots.

spots: Three kinds of cone cells sense mostly red, green or blue light. Your brain mixes their signals into every colour.
Rods work in dim light but don't see colour. That's why everything looks grey at night.
About 1 in 12 boys of European ancestry (and far fewer girls) have one kind of cone that works differently, so some colours look alike.
Has 12 or more kinds of colour detectors, but in tests it's actually worse than us at telling close colours apart!

sec.t:
Because [[@brain-works|the brain]] compares three signals, it can tell apart a huge number of shades, perhaps a million or more. The idea that colour vision uses just three [[sensor|sensors]] was suggested by the English scientist Thomas Young around 1802, long before anyone could see a cone cell.

A phone or TV uses the same trick in reverse. Every [[@pixels|pixel]] is made of tiny red, green and blue lights. Turn them up and down in different amounts, and your cones can't tell the mix from the real thing. Adding coloured light works differently from [[@crayons-paints|mixing paints]], as you can see in [[@colour-mix|mixing colours]].

Many animals see fewer colours than we do. Deer, like most [[mammal|mammals]], have only two kinds of cones. To them, a [[@tiger-stripes|tiger's]] orange coat blends into green leaves. That may be why tigers can be bright orange and still sneak up on their prey.

Bulls are similar. A matador's red cape doesn't make a bull angry because it's red. The bull charges at the movement. Dogs, too, see a world mostly of blues and yellows, which is why a red ball on green grass can be hard for them to spot.

Many birds, fish and insects have four kinds of cones, including one that senses [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light, which we can't see at all. Bees spot ultraviolet patterns on flowers that guide them to the [[nectar|nectar]], like landing lights on a runway.

[[@power-mantis-shrimp|The mantis shrimp]] has 12 or more kinds of colour detectors. Yet tests show it's worse than people at telling close colours apart. It seems to recognise colours quickly rather than compare them carefully, the way our brains do. Some [[@octopus-smart|octopuses]] are even stranger: they [[@octopus-colour|change colour brilliantly]] but seem to have only one kind of light sensor.

At night, your cones give up and your rods take over. Rods are very sensitive but can't tell colours apart. That's why a red rose and a green leaf both look grey by moonlight, and why it takes your eyes several minutes to adjust when you walk into a dark room. sec.t:
कलमकारी की कलम बाँस की एक नुकीली डंडी होती है, जिसकी नोक के पास ऊन या कपड़े की एक गद्दी लिपटी रहती है। गद्दी रंग सोख लेती है और उसे धीरे-धीरे नोक तक पहुँचाती है, जैसे फ़ाउंटेन पेन में स्याही।

काली रेखाओं के लिए कलाकार एक खास घोल बनाते हैं। इसके लिए लोहे के [[oxidation|ज़ंग]] लगे टुकड़ों को [[@jaggery|गुड़]] और पानी में कई दिन तक भिगोकर रखा जाता है। इसकी गंध तेज़ होती है, पर यह गहरा और पक्का काला रंग देता है। श्रीकालहस्ती के कपड़े की बहुत-सी बारीक रेखाएँ बिना किसी खाके के, सीधे हाथ से खींची जाती हैं।

मछलीपट्टनम में काम का तरीका अलग है। कारीगर लकड़ी के ठप्पों पर, अक्सर सागौन के, डिज़ाइन खोदते हैं और उन्हें एक के बाद एक कपड़े पर छापते जाते हैं। एक डिज़ाइन के लिए कई ठप्पे लग सकते हैं, एक बाहरी रेखा के लिए और एक-एक हर रंग के लिए। इन्हें बिल्कुल ठीक जगह पर बिठाने के लिए सधा हुआ हाथ और पैनी नज़र चाहिए। बारीक काम अक्सर अब भी कलम से हाथ से ही किया जाता है।

sec.h: जिस कपड़े ने यूरोप जीत लिया
sec.t:
सदियों तक भारत के पूर्वी तट के रंगे और छपे सूती कपड़ों का व्यापार एशिया, अफ़्रीका और यूरोप तक होता रहा। मछलीपट्टनम एक [[@sea-ports|चहल-पहल वाला बंदरगाह]] था, और इसके ठप्पा-छपाई वाले डिज़ाइनों को फ़ारस के खरीदारों और आज के [[@hyderabad|हैदराबाद]] के पास गोलकुंडा के दरबार की पसंद ने गढ़ा।

1600 के दशक में जब [[@east-india-company|ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी]] समेत यूरोपीय व्यापारी ये चटख, धुलने वाले कपड़े अपने देश ले गए, तो लोग कपड़ों, परदों और चादरों के लिए इन पर फ़िदा हो गए। यूरोप में ऐसा कुछ था ही नहीं। वहाँ के रेशम और ऊन के बुनकरों को अपनी रोज़ी छिनने का डर सताने लगा। फ़्रांस ने 1686 में भारतीय छपे सूती कपड़ों के [[import|आयात]] पर पाबंदी लगा दी, और ब्रिटेन ने 1700 और 1721 में इनके खिलाफ़ अपने कानून बनाए।

भारतीय रंगरेज़ों ने लंबे समय तक अपने राज़ छिपाए रखे, पर आखिरकार यूरोप की फ़ैक्टरियों ने मशीनों से यह रूप नकल करना सीख लिया। कलमकारी लगभग गायब होने लगी थी, पर 20वीं सदी में हस्तशिल्प संस्थाओं और डिज़ाइनरों की मदद से इसे फिर से जीवन मिला।

आज यह तुम्हें साड़ियों, कुर्तों, दीवार पर टाँगने वाले कपड़ों और कुशन कवर पर दिख सकती है। कुछ कारीगर अब समय बचाने के लिए [[@accident-mauve|रासायनिक रंग]] इस्तेमाल करते हैं, तो कुछ अब भी धीमी, कुदरती प्रक्रिया पर टिके हैं। श्रीकालहस्ती और मछलीपट्टनम, दोनों शैलियों को जीआई टैग मिला है। यह सरकार का एक ठप्पा है जो किसी खास जगह से जुड़े उत्पाद की रक्षा करता है, जैसे दार्जिलिंग की चाय।

text: विन्सेंट वान गॉग (1853–1890) [[@amsterdam|नीदरलैंड्स के चित्रकार]] थे, जो कूची के मोटे, घुमड़ते स्ट्रोक और गहरे, चटक रंगों के लिए मशहूर हैं। उन्होंने सूरजमुखी, गेहूँ के खेत, तारों भरे आसमान, अपना कमरा, और अपने और आसपास के लोगों के दर्जनों चित्र बनाए।

अपनी छोटी-सी ज़िंदगी में वे ग़रीब रहे, अक्सर अकेले रहे, और गंभीर बीमारी के ऐसे दौरों से जूझते रहे जिनका असर उनके मन पर पड़ता था। उनकी बिक्री बहुत कम हुई। उनके भाई थियो सालों तक पैसों और चिट्ठियों से उनका साथ देते रहे। विन्सेंट की मौत के बाद उनकी पेंटिंग धीरे-धीरे दुनिया भर में मशहूर हुईं। आज वे कहीं भी सबसे कीमती और सबसे प्यारी तस्वीरों में गिनी जाती हैं।

sec.t:
वान गॉग नीदरलैंड्स के दक्षिण में एक पादरी के बेटे के रूप में पले-बढ़े। कलाकार बनने से पहले उन्होंने कई काम आज़माए। उन्होंने एक कला-व्यापारी के यहाँ नौकरी की, इंग्लैंड के एक स्कूल में पढ़ाया, किताबें बेचीं, और बेल्जियम में कोयला खदान मज़दूरों के बीच उपदेशक बनने की तालीम ली।

27 साल की उम्र में उन्होंने कलाकार बनने का फ़ैसला किया। उन्होंने ज़्यादातर नकल करके, बार-बार चित्र बनाने का अभ्यास करके ख़ुद सीखा। उनकी शुरुआती पेंटिंग गहरी और मिट्टी जैसे रंगों वाली थीं, किसानों और बुनकरों से भरी। एक मशहूर पेंटिंग, *द पोटैटो ईटर्स*, एक परिवार को एक ही लैंप की रोशनी में रात का खाना खाते दिखाती है।

1888 में वान गॉग धूप से भरे दक्षिणी फ़्रांस के आर्ल शहर आ गए। उन्होंने पीले रंग से पुता एक घर किराए पर लिया और वहाँ कलाकारों की एक बस्ती बसाने का सपना देखा। साल भर से कुछ ज़्यादा समय में उन्होंने लगभग 200 पेंटिंग बनाईं, जिनमें मशहूर *सनफ़्लावर्स* भी है।

चित्रकार पॉल गोगाँ उनके साथ रहने आए, पर दोनों में ज़बरदस्त बहस हुई। इसके बाद वान गॉग की हालत बहुत बिगड़ गई और उन्होंने अपने ही कान को चोट पहुँचा ली। फिर उन्होंने सेंट-रेमी के एक अस्पताल में एक साल बिताया, जहाँ वे बग़ीचों, जैतून के पेड़ों और अपनी खिड़की से दिखते नज़ारों को रंगते रहे।

जून 1889 में उसी अस्पताल के कमरे से वान गॉग ने *द स्टारी नाइट* बनाई। एक गाँव घुमड़ती हवा, दमकते तारों और हँसिये जैसे चाँद से भरे आसमान के नीचे सो रहा है, और एक गहरे रंग का सरू का पेड़ लौ की तरह ऊपर उठ रहा है।

उन्होंने इसे कुछ याद से और कुछ कल्पना से बनाया, ठीक वैसा नहीं जैसा उन्होंने देखा था। [[astronomer|खगोलविदों]] ने बताया है कि क्षितिज के पास का चमकीला "तारा" शायद [[@venus-hot|शुक्र ग्रह]] है, जो तब सुबह-सवेरे आसमान में दिखता था। यह पेंटिंग अब [[@new-york|न्यूयॉर्क]] के म्यूज़ियम ऑफ़ [[@modern-art|मॉडर्न आर्ट]] में टँगी है।

विन्सेंट ने सैकड़ों चिट्ठियाँ लिखीं, ज़्यादातर थियो को। इनमें से 800 से ज़्यादा बची हैं। इनमें वे बताते हैं कि क्या बना रहे हैं, कौन से रंग इस्तेमाल कर रहे हैं और क्यों, और कैसा महसूस कर रहे हैं। उनकी ज़िंदगी और सोच के बारे में हम इतना कुछ जानते हैं, उसकी एक वजह ये चिट्ठियाँ हैं।

लंबी बीमारी के बाद जुलाई 1890 में 37 साल की उम्र में वान गॉग की मृत्यु हो गई। थियो की मौत बस छह महीने बाद हुई। थियो की विधवा, यो वान गॉग-बोंगर, ने पेंटिंग और चिट्ठियाँ सँभालकर रखीं, प्रदर्शनियाँ लगवाईं और चिट्ठियाँ छपवाईं। उनके बिना शायद दुनिया कभी उनका काम जान ही न पाती। आज एम्स्टर्डम के वान गॉग म्यूज़ियम में उनकी पेंटिंग का सबसे बड़ा संग्रह है, और यह यूरोप के सबसे ज़्यादा देखे जाने वाले [[@museums|संग्रहालयों]] में से है।

text: Every five years, India elects the 543 members of its Lok Sabha, the house of Parliament that chooses the government. In 2024, about 97 crore people were registered to vote, more than the populations of the USA and the European Union put together. About 64 crore of them actually voted.

Running it is a huge job. The [[@election-commission|Election Commission]] sets up more than ten lakh polling stations, trains crores of officials, and moves electronic voting machines across mountains, rivers and deserts. Voting is spread over several weeks and phases. Then, on one day, all the votes are counted, and the results come in within hours.

st.prompt: How many days did India's 2024 general election take, from the first day of voting to the last?
st.reveal: Voting took place in seven phases between 19 April and 1 June 2024, 44 days in all. Spreading it out lets security forces and election staff move from state to state. All the votes were then counted on a single day, 4 June.

d.try: Run an election at home or in class for something small, like a class pet's name. Make a list of voters, set up a hidden corner for voting, mark each voter's finger with a washable pen so nobody votes twice, and count the votes in front of everyone. Notice how each rule makes cheating harder.
myth: In a country as big and poor as India was in 1951, a fair national election was impossible.

Many experts doubted it at the time, because most voters could not read. India used party symbols on ballots so anyone could vote, and the first general election in 1951–52 was widely seen as a success.

sec.t:
The rule is that no voter should have to travel more than about 2 km to reach a polling station. That leads to some unusual booths.

For many years, a polling station was set up at Banej, deep in Gujarat's [[@lions-gir|Gir forest]], for one voter: a priest named Bharatdas Darshandas, who looked after a temple there. A team of officials travelled through lion country to set up the booth just for him. Elsewhere, staff have hiked for days to reach Himalayan villages, crossed rivers on boats in Assam and ridden camels in the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]]. One polling station at Tashigang in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], at about 4,650 metres, is among the highest in the world.

Voters line up, show an identity card and have their name checked against the voters' list. An official paints a line of purple indelible ink on the left index finger, which lasts for days and stops anyone voting twice. Inside the booth, the voter presses a button next to a candidate's name and symbol on the electronic voting machine.

A small printer called a VVPAT shows a paper slip for about seven seconds, so voters can check that their choice was recorded. Since 2013, voters can also choose NOTA, "None of the Above", if they don't want any candidate.

In 2024, voting took place in seven phases, from 19 April to 1 June. On 4 June, the machines were opened and counted across the country. Because the machines store the votes electronically, most results were known by that evening.

The party or group of parties that wins a majority of Lok Sabha seats, at least 272, forms the government, and its leader becomes Prime Minister. Turnout in 2024 was about 66 per cent, and, for only the second time, women voted at a slightly higher rate than men. Every citizen aged 18 or over gets the same single vote, rich or poor, in a city flat or a forest temple. That simple rule is what [[@vote-how|voting]] in any [[democracy|democracy]] rests on, and India applies it on a scale nobody else has tried.

text: Mountain rescue teams find and help people who are lost, hurt or stuck in the mountains. When someone calls for help, the team gathers fast. They work out where the person might be, then go in on foot, on skis, by helicopter or with search dogs.

Once they reach the person, they give first aid, keep them warm and carry them out, often on a stretcher lowered down cliffs by ropes. In the USA and Britain, many rescuers are trained volunteers. In India and Nepal, rescues often involve the army, the air force, local guides and special disaster teams.

st.prompt: Someone is buried by an avalanche. Within roughly how long must rescuers dig them out to give them the best chance?
st.reveal: Most buried people survive if found within about 15 minutes, but the chances drop quickly after about half an hour. That is why skiers carry beacons, probes and shovels, so friends can dig without waiting for help.

src: Himalayan Rescue Association Nepal, history and aid posts.

d.try: Play a beacon game. Hide a small ticking kitchen timer or a phone playing quiet music under cushions. With eyes covered, a friend must find it by sound alone while you time them. Now try it with three hidden objects and see how much longer it takes.
myth: St Bernard rescue dogs carried little barrels of brandy around their necks.

The monks of the Great St Bernard Hospice say their dogs never carried brandy barrels. The idea seems to come from a painting by the English artist Edwin Landseer in the 1820s. Alcohol is also a bad idea for someone who is freezing.

sec.t:
Mountains punish delay. Cold, injury and thin air all get worse with time. For avalanches, the numbers are stark. Most people buried in snow survive if dug out within about 15 minutes. After about 35 minutes, the chances fall steeply.

So the first rescuers are often the victim's own friends. Skiers and climbers carry avalanche beacons, small radios that beep to show where a buried person lies. They also carry folding probes to poke through the snow and shovels to dig. A good team can find and dig out a person in minutes.

On popular routes in Nepal, the Himalayan Rescue Association runs aid posts staffed by volunteer doctors. Its clinic at Pheriche, on the trail to [[@everest-base-camp|Everest Base Camp]], has treated trekkers suffering from altitude sickness since the 1970s. Every season, the doctors give talks to walkers about the danger signs.

The best cure for altitude sickness is simple: go down. Even a few hundred metres lower can make a big difference, as the science of [[@altitude|altitude]] explains. Sherpa guides and porters, who know the mountains best, often carry out rescues long before any helicopter arrives.

Search dogs can sniff out a person buried under snow or rubble far faster than a line of people with probes. A trained avalanche dog can search an area in minutes that would take a team hours. Dogs smell the tiny traces of scent that rise through the snow, then dig furiously at the spot. Many ski resorts in the Alps and the Rockies keep dogs on duty all winter, sometimes riding chairlifts with their handlers.

The most famous mountain dog is Barry, a St Bernard who lived at the Great St Bernard Hospice in the Swiss Alps in the early 1800s. Monks there had kept dogs to guide travellers through the snowy pass. Barry is credited with saving about 40 people. His preserved body is now in a museum in Bern.

Rescuers say most rescues could be avoided with simple steps. Tell someone where you are going and when you'll be back. Carry warm clothes, water, a torch and a charged phone. Turn back if the weather turns.

They also ask people to learn basic [[@first-aid|first aid]], because the person who helps first is usually a friend, not a rescuer. Barry was one of many animal heroes, and the stories of [[@oddity-dogs-history|dogs who changed history]] include a few more who saved lives.

text: For thousands of years, India measured with its own units. Gold and spices were weighed in ratti, masha and tola. Rice and wheat were sold by the ser and the maund. Cloth was measured in gaj, land in bigha, and long distances in kos.

These units grew from everyday things: seeds, hands, arms and footsteps. They worked well inside one town or kingdom. But a ser in one market might not match a ser in the next, and that made trade and taxes messy.

After independence, India switched to the [[@metric-system|metric system]], with grams, metres and litres. The change began with a law in 1956 and took several years. Some old units still survive, especially at the jeweller's.

st.prompt: In the old system, how many annas made one rupee?
st.reveal: A rupee was 16 annas, and each anna was 4 paise, so a rupee was 64 old paise. In 1957 India switched to decimal coins, with 100 naye paise to the rupee.

d.try: Ask a grandparent or older neighbour which old units they remember, such as seer, maund, gaj or bigha. Write down what each was used for and roughly how big it was. Then work out each one in grams, metres or square metres, and see whose memory matches the numbers.
myth: A bigha is the same size everywhere in India.

The bigha is a traditional land unit, and its size varies a lot from state to state and even district to district. In some places it's about a third of an acre, in others more than half an acre, so land papers always need checking.
facts: cubes of stone in a doubling series, over 4,000 years old

sec.t:
Long before kings and coins, the [[@harappan-trade|Harappan]] cities of the Indus valley used carefully cut cubes of stone, often a pale banded rock called chert, as weights. They have been found from Gujarat to Pakistan, and they match each other closely.

The smaller weights double each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 units. Larger ones jump in tens. That doubling is the same idea computers use in [[@binary-code|binary]] counting.

At Lothal in Gujarat, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found a scale made of ivory with fine lines cut into it, used for measuring length. Matching weights across a huge area suggests a shared system that traders trusted.

{{story:harappan-trade}}

Goldsmiths needed tiny, reliable weights. One answer was the seed of the gunja vine, bright red with a black spot. Gunja seeds are fairly even in size, so the ratti, from the Sanskrit *raktika*, linked to the word for red, became a unit of about a tenth of a gram.

From the ratti came bigger units. Eight ratti made a masha, and twelve masha made a tola. In British India the tola was fixed at 180 grains, about 11.66 grams. The silver rupee coin itself was minted to weigh one tola.

Even today, many people talk about the price of gold "per tola". In practice, jewellers often round it to 10 grams.

For grain and vegetables, people used the ser and the maund. In British India the standard ser was 80 tola, a little under a kilogram, and 40 ser made a maund, about 37 kilograms. But local sers were often different.

Lengths came from the body too. A *hasta* was roughly an arm's length from elbow to fingertip. The Mughal emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] set an official yard, the *Ilahi gaz*, for measuring land so taxes would be fair. The gaj is still used for cloth and plots in north India.

Money had its own maths. A rupee was split into 16 annas, each anna into 4 paise, and each paisa into 3 pies. So a rupee held 192 pies. Prices like "two annas" or "four annas" were common in shops and in songs.

On 1 April 1957 India went [[decimal|decimal]], with 100 naye paise ("new paise") to the rupee. The word "naye" was dropped in 1964.

The Standards of Weights and Measures Act of 1956 made the metric system India's official system. Shops had to switch to kilograms and metres over the next few years. Teachers ran classes and posters explained the new units. For years, many people kept converting in their heads.

Old habits stay, though. Farmers still talk in bigha and acre, gold is still bought by the tola, and people in many towns still say "one ser" when they mean about a kilo. Big numbers are still counted the Indian way, in [[@lakh-crore|lakhs and crores]].

text: Pi is the number you get when you divide the distance around a circle, its circumference, by the distance across it, its [[diameter|diameter]]. It does not matter how big the circle is. The answer is always the same: about 3.14159. Mathematicians write it with the Greek letter π.

Pi's [[@decimals|decimals]] go on forever and never fall into a repeating pattern. Computers have worked out more than a hundred trillion digits, and no pattern has ever appeared. Pi turns up all over maths and science, wherever [[@circles|circles]], spheres, waves or spinning things are involved.

st.prompt: How many decimal places of pi do NASA engineers use to steer spacecraft through the solar system?
st.reveal: About 15 decimal places is enough to work out a spacecraft's path with an error of just a few centimetres over billions of kilometres. Using 3.14 alone would make big mistakes, but thousands of digits would be pointless.

src: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (2016), "How Many Decimals of Pi Do We Really Need?"
Plofker K. (2009) Mathematics in India. Princeton University Press.
Britannica, "Pi".

d.try: Find five round things, like a plate, a bangle, a jar lid and a bucket. Wrap a piece of string around each one, then measure the string with a ruler. Measure the width across the middle too. Divide the distance around by the width, using a calculator if you like. Your answers should all be close to 3.1.
myth: Pi is exactly 22/7.

22/7 is 3.142857..., a handy approximation that is correct to two decimal places. Pi is 3.14159... and cannot be written exactly as any fraction. Archimedes showed over 2,000 years ago that 22/7 is slightly too big.

sec.h: Why it is always the same
sec.t:
All circles are the same shape. A small circle is just a big circle shrunk down, so the ratio between around and across never changes. Double the width of a circle and you double the distance around it too.

People noticed long ago that the distance around was a bit more than three times the width. The Bible describes a round tank about three times as far around as across. Ancient Egyptian and Babylonian scribes used values close to 3.16 and 3.125. Close enough for building, but not quite right.

Around 250 BCE, the Greek mathematician Archimedes, who lived in Syracuse on the island of Sicily, found a clever way to pin pi down. He drew shapes with straight sides inside and outside a circle. The circle had to be bigger than the inner shape and smaller than the outer one. Using shapes with 96 sides, he showed that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7, or about 3.1408 and 3.1429. Much of the maths of [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]] worked in this careful way.

{{story:ancient-greece}}

In 499 CE, the Indian [[astronomer|astronomer]] [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] gave a value for pi that works out to 3.1416. He also described it as approximate, which some historians take as a hint that he knew it could not be written exactly.

Around 1400, [[@madhava|Madhava of Sangamagrama]], a mathematician in [[@kerala|Kerala]], found a way to calculate pi using an endless sum of [[@fractions|fractions]]. Mathematicians in Europe found similar formulas about 250 years later. Much later, in the early 1900s, Srinivasa Ramanujan discovered formulas that produce many correct digits of pi very quickly. Versions of them are still used in record-breaking computer calculations.

In 1761, the Swiss mathematician Johann Lambert proved that pi is irrational. That means it can never be written exactly as one whole number divided by another. Its [[decimal|decimals]] go on forever with no repeating pattern. In 1882 it was shown to be even stranger. No simple equation with whole numbers can produce it. That means you cannot construct a square with exactly the same area as a circle using only a ruler and compass.

The symbol π was first used for this number by the Welsh mathematician William Jones in 1706. It became popular after the great Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler used it.

In the United States, people write dates month first, so 14 March is 3/14. Many schools celebrate it as [[@maths-pi-day|Pi Day]], often by eating pie. It is also [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]]'s birthday.

In 1897 a bill in Indiana tried to set a wrong value for pi by law, after a local doctor claimed he had solved an ancient circle puzzle. It passed one part of the [[@governors-states|state government]] before a visiting mathematics professor helped stop it. The value of pi, like all of maths, cannot be decided by voting.

text: Plenty of maths problems have never been solved, and some are very easy to state. An unsolved problem is one where nobody has managed to prove the answer, even if they strongly suspect what it is.

Checking examples isn't enough in maths. A computer might test a rule on billions of numbers, but a proof must show the rule works for every number, forever. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute in the USA picked seven of the hardest open questions and offered 1 million dollars for each. As of 2026, only one has been solved.

st.prompt: In the Collatz puzzle, you halve even numbers and turn odd numbers into 3 × n + 1. Start at 6. Where do you end up?
st.reveal: 6 goes to 3, then 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, and then 4, 2, 1 again forever. Every number ever tested ends in that loop, but nobody has proved that all numbers must.

src: Clay Mathematics Institute, the Millennium Prize Problems.
Simon Singh, Fermat's Last Theorem (1997).

d.try: Pick any whole number and play the Collatz game. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Keep going until you reach 1, counting the steps. Try 7 and then 27, which takes 111 steps and climbs as high as 9,232 on the way.
myth: By now, mathematicians have worked everything out, so maths is finished.
Maths has more open questions than ever. Every solved problem tends to raise new ones, and thousands of new results are published every year.

sec.t:
Take any whole number. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add 1. Repeat. Start with 7 and you go 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

The German mathematician Lothar Collatz suggested in 1937 that every starting number eventually reaches 1. [[@computers-how|Computers]] have checked every starting number into the hundreds of billions of billions, and every single one gets there. That's the sort of question a machine can test quickly but never settle. Yet nobody can prove it must always happen. Some numbers soar high before falling, like 27, which climbs past 9,000.

In 1742, Christian Goldbach wrote a letter to the great mathematician [[@puzzle-konigsberg|Leonhard Euler]] with a guess. Every even number bigger than 2, he suggested, is the sum of two [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]]. So 8 = 3 + 5, 20 = 7 + 13, and 100 = 47 + 53.

Computers have checked this for every even number up to about 4 followed by 18 zeros. It has never failed. But nearly three centuries later, there is still no proof.

A cousin of this puzzle asks whether there are endless twin primes, pairs only 2 apart like 11 and 13. In 2013, Yitang Zhang, a little-known lecturer in the USA, proved that prime pairs never stop appearing within some fixed gap. It was a huge step, though the gap he could prove was 70 million, not 2.

{{story:supercomputers}}

One of the Clay problems, the Poincaré conjecture, was about the possible shapes of three-dimensional space. In 2002 and 2003, the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman posted his solution online. Experts spent years checking it and agreed he was right.

He was offered the Fields Medal, often called the top prize in maths, and later the million dollars. He declined both and largely withdrew from public life. He said he was not interested in money or fame.

Old problems do fall. Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat scribbled a note in the margin of a book. He claimed a marvellous proof of a statement about powers of numbers, but said the margin was too small to hold it. Nobody found a proof for about 350 years. In 1994, the British mathematician Andrew Wiles finally completed one, after working on it mostly in secret for seven years.

[[@ramanujan|Srinivasa Ramanujan]] left notebooks full of formulas without proofs. Mathematicians spent decades proving them, and some led to whole new fields. Others are still waiting. The Riemann [[hypothesis|hypothesis]], a question about how the primes are spread out, was posed in 1859 and is one of the six Clay problems that remain open.

text: Magicians fool us by playing tricks on our attention and memory. Your brain cannot take in everything your eyes see, so it picks out what seems important and ignores the rest. A good magician decides what you will think is important.

The key skill is misdirection, guiding your attention away from the secret move. Magicians also use sleight of hand, fast and smooth finger skills practised for years, and hidden props such as false bottoms and secret pockets. Your [[@brain-works|brain]] fills in the gaps, and the trick seems impossible.

st.prompt: When a magician wants you to look away from their left hand, what usually works best?

options.t: Moving the right hand in a big curve
Telling you not to look at the left hand
Moving both hands very fast in straight lines

st.reveal: Scientists have found that our eyes tend to follow a hand moving in a curve, and to jump about with straight, fast movements. Magicians use curved movements to guide your attention exactly where they want it.

src: Simons and Chabris (1999), Gorillas in our midst, Perception.
Peter Lamont, The Rise of the Indian Rope Trick (2004).
Macknik, Martinez-Conde and Blakeslee, Sleights of Mind (2010).

d.try: Learn the classic French drop with a coin. Hold the coin in one hand, pretend to take it with the other, but let it drop secretly into your palm. Then watch the empty hand closely yourself as you "open" it. Practise in a mirror until your eyes follow the wrong hand too.
myth: Magicians in India once performed the rope trick, making a boy climb a rope into thin air and vanish.
Historians have found no reliable eyewitness accounts. The story spread widely after an 1890 article in the Chicago Tribune, which the newspaper later admitted was a hoax.
facts: misdirection, sleight of hand, hidden props

sec.t:
Magicians know where your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] will go. People look where the magician looks, so a performer can glance at one hand while the other does the secret move. A sudden noise, a joke or a question also grabs attention for a moment.

Researchers have found that a hand moving in a smooth curve draws the eyes better than a hand moving in a straight line. Magicians discovered this long before scientists did, simply by practising in front of audiences.

Some tricks work after they are over. Magicians describe what happened in a slightly wrong way, and people remember the description instead of what they saw. A shuffled deck is called "your deck", and a card the magician actually chose becomes "the card you picked".

Our [[@memory|memory]] is not a recording. It is rebuilt every time we remember, and small suggestions can change it. Many people leave a show sure they saw something that never happened.

The Frenchman Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, who lived in the 1800s, is often called the father of modern magic. He wore ordinary evening clothes instead of wizard robes and performed in a theatre like a gentleman scientist. The American escape artist Harry Houdini took his stage name from him.

In India, [[@pop-magic-shows|P. C. Sorcar]] became world famous in the mid-1900s for grand stage shows, including making a person appear to be sawn in half. Street magicians across India have long performed tricks with cups and balls, a routine so old that versions of it appear in writings from [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]].

sec.h: The rope trick that never was
sec.t:
For more than a century, people around the world have heard of the Indian rope trick. A magician throws a rope into the air, it stays standing, and a boy climbs up and vanishes. The historian Peter Lamont traced the story and found it took off after an 1890 article in the *Chicago Tribune*.

The newspaper later admitted the article was invented. Since then, many people have offered prizes for anyone who could perform the trick in the open air. No one has claimed them. The rope trick shows how a good story can fool people as well as any magician.

text: From the 1920s to the 1960s, radio was the main way families heard news, music and stories. A radio set was often a big wooden cabinet that took pride of place in the living room. Everyone gathered around it at fixed times, the way people later gathered around a TV.

Radio worked by turning sound into invisible [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] that travelled through the air from a tall transmitter. A receiver in each home turned the waves back into sound. Anyone in range could listen for free, at the same moment, whether they lived in a city flat or a farmhouse.

st.prompt: In 1938, an American radio play pretended Martians were landing in New Jersey. What really happened afterwards?

options.t: Most listeners knew it was a play, but newspapers reported a giant panic
Millions of people fled their homes in cars

sec.t:
The first regular radio station in the USA, KDKA in Pittsburgh, went on air in 1920 by announcing election results. Within a few years, there were hundreds of stations. Early sets used glass valves, a bit like small [[@light-bulb|light bulbs]], that took time to warm up and glowed orange in the dark.

Radio brought live events into homes for the first time. Families heard boxing matches, concerts and, during the 1930s, President Franklin Roosevelt's "fireside chats", in which he spoke calmly to the nation about hard times.

In 1952, Radio Ceylon, broadcasting from Colombo in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], began a weekly show of Hindi [[@film-songs|film songs]] called *Binaca Geetmala*. Its host, Ameen Sayani, greeted listeners with "Behno aur bhaiyon" (sisters and brothers), and counted down the most popular songs of the week.

It ran for decades and became one of the best-loved radio shows in Asia. Families tuned in every Wednesday night to find out which song was at number one. All India Radio answered with its own film music channel, Vividh Bharati, in 1957.

In the 1950s, the [[transistor|transistor]], a tiny electronic switch, replaced bulky valves. Radios became small, cheap and battery-powered. Teenagers could carry one to the beach, farmers could hang one from a tree in the field, and cricket fans could hold one to their ear at the ground.

In India, the small "transistor", as people called it, became a common wedding gift and a prized family possession. In many homes it was the first electronic device anyone owned.

When TV arrived, many people expected radio to disappear. It did not. People kept listening in cars, kitchens and shops. FM radio, with clearer sound, spread across Indian cities in the 2000s, along with chatty radio jockeys.

Community radio stations now broadcast in local languages to villages, run by local groups and colleges. And the old habit of listening to a voice tell a story has found a new home in [[@podcasts|podcasts]], which you can play whenever you like.

text: Shooting is an Olympic sport because it tests skills that are very hard to master: stillness, precision and calm under pressure. It has been part of the modern [[@olympics|Olympics]] since the first Games in Athens in 1896. Its roots are in hunting and the military, but as a sport it is about hitting paper or electronic targets and clay discs, never living things.

Olympic shooting has three main kinds: rifle, pistol and shotgun. Athletes compete at set distances, such as 10, 25 and 50 metres. Ranges have strict safety rules, and coaches, judges and range officers watch every shot.

sec.t:
In the 10-metre air rifle event, the target's centre "10" ring is a dot just 0.5 millimetres across. Electronic targets measure where each pellet lands, even scoring tenths of a point, like 10.6 or 10.9.

At 10 metres, that is like hitting a grain of sand at the far end of a classroom. To do it, shooters wear stiff jackets and special shoes to stay steady. They aim through sights, breathe slowly and press the trigger so gently that the rifle barely moves.

On 11 August 2008, in Beijing, Abhinav Bindra won the 10-metre air rifle. It was India's first ever individual Olympic gold medal. He was so focused that he barely smiled at first.

Bindra had trained for years, even practising on a range his family built at home. Four years earlier, in Athens, the army officer Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore had won silver in double trap, a shotgun event. These two medals helped make shooting one of India's most successful Olympic sports. Bindra later wrote that after winning he felt strangely empty, because the goal he had chased for years was suddenly gone. Many athletes say the same.

In 2012 Gagan Narang won bronze and Vijay Kumar silver in London. Then came a long gap. In Paris in 2024 India's shooters came back strongly.

Manu Bhaker, from Haryana, won bronze in the 10-metre air pistol and another bronze with Sarabjot Singh in the mixed team event. She became the first Indian since independence to win two medals at the same Olympics. Swapnil Kusale added a third bronze, in the 50-metre rifle three positions event, where shooters fire kneeling, lying down and standing.

In shotgun events, machines fling orange clay discs through the air at high speed. Shooters must swing, aim and fire in less than a second. A shotgun fires a spread of tiny pellets, which helps hit a fast-moving disc.

Shooting has been popular in the USA for a long time. American shooters such as Kim Rhode have won Olympic medals at six Games in a row. As with archery, the target is always the challenge, and the best shooters say the hardest opponent is their own nerves.

text: चेहरा तब लाल होता है जब शरीर अचानक ढेर सारा [[adrenaline|एड्रेनलिन]] छोड़ता है। यह वही रसायन है जिसकी वजह से डर के मारे “लड़ो या भागो” वाला एहसास होता है। एड्रेनलिन गालों, कानों और गर्दन की नन्ही खून की नलियों को चौड़ा कर देता है। त्वचा की सतह के पास ज़्यादा खून बहने लगता है, इसलिए वह गुलाबी हो जाती है और गर्म लगती है।
चेहरा अक्सर झेंप, शर्मीलेपन या लज्जा जैसी [[@emotions|भावनाओं]] के साथ लाल होता है। तुम कोशिश करके इसे बंद नहीं कर सकते। उल्टा, लाल होने की फ़िक्र करने से अक्सर यह और बढ़ जाता है।
बड़ी पहेली यह है कि इंसानों का चेहरा लाल होता ही क्यों है। कोई और जानवर ऐसा करता नहीं दिखता। वैज्ञानिकों को लगता है कि यह दूसरों के लिए एक इशारा हो सकता है कि हमें पता है, हमसे चूक हो गई।

तुम्हारे चेहरे में [[@blood|खून]] की छोटी-छोटी नलियाँ भरी हुई हैं, और उनमें से कई सतह के बहुत पास हैं। गालों की त्वचा भी पतली होती है। इसलिए वहाँ खून के बहाव में ज़रा-सा बदलाव भी आसानी से दिख जाता है।

जब तुम्हें शर्म आती है, तो तुम्हारा [[nerve|तंत्रिका तंत्र]] कुछ ही सेकंड में हरकत में आ जाता है। एड्रेनलिन छूटता है, और चेहरे की [[vein|शिराएँ]] और छोटी नलियाँ और खुल जाती हैं। खून तेज़ी से भीतर आता है। गाल एक डिग्री या उससे ज़्यादा गर्म हो सकते हैं, जिसे गर्मी नापने वाले कैमरे पकड़ लेते हैं।

ज़्यादातर बार लाली कुछ ही मिनटों में उतर जाती है। कुछ लोगों का चेहरा तब भी लाल होता है जब कोई उनकी तारीफ़ कर दे या अचानक कोई अच्छी बात कह दे, न कि सिर्फ़ तब जब कुछ गड़बड़ हो। अच्छा ध्यान भी इसे जगा सकता है। कसरत, गर्म मौसम या तीखा खाना भी चेहरा लाल कर सकता है, पर वह अलग तरह की लाली है, जो भावनाओं से नहीं, गर्मी से जुड़ी है।

1872 में चार्ल्स डार्विन ने एक किताब लिखी कि इंसान और जानवर अपनी भावनाएँ कैसे दिखाते हैं। उन्होंने शर्म से चेहरा लाल होने को “सारे भावों में सबसे अनोखा और सबसे इंसानी” कहा। उन्होंने देखा कि हर जगह लोगों का चेहरा लाल होता है, और जो देख नहीं सकते, उनका भी। इसका मतलब था कि यह दूसरों को देखकर सीखी गई चीज़ नहीं है।

लगभग 25 साल बाद अमेरिकी लेखक [[@mark-twain|मार्क ट्वेन]] ने चुटकी ली: “इंसान ही अकेला ऐसा जानवर है जो शरमाता है। या जिसे शरमाने की ज़रूरत पड़ती है।”

बच्चों का चेहरा लगभग दो से चार साल की उम्र में लाल होना शुरू होता लगता है, लगभग उसी समय जब उन्हें समझ आने लगता है कि दूसरे उन्हें कैसे देखते हैं। इससे लगता है कि चेहरा लाल होना इस सोच से जुड़ा है कि दूसरे हमारे बारे में क्या सोचते हैं।

{{story:empathy}}

एक बड़ा विचार यह है। अगर तुम कोई नियम तोड़ो या गलती करो, तो गालों की लाली दूसरों को बताती है कि तुम्हें पता है और तुम्हें बुरा लग रहा है। इससे शायद वे तुम्हें जल्दी माफ़ कर दें।

प्रयोग इस बात का साथ देते हैं। नीदरलैंड्स के मनोवैज्ञानिकों ने लोगों को किसी ऐसे व्यक्ति की तस्वीरें और किस्से दिखाए जिसने गलती की थी। जब उस व्यक्ति का चेहरा लाल था, तो देखने वालों ने उस पर ज़्यादा भरोसा किया और उसके बारे में ज़्यादा नरमी से राय बनाई। लाली मानो बिना बोले कहा गया “सॉरी” थी।

हो सकता है चेहरा लाल होना उस तरीके का हिस्सा हो जिससे इंसान झुंड में रहते हैं और मिल-जुलकर चलते हैं। यह [[@empathy|हमदर्दी]] से जुड़ता है, यानी दूसरों की भावनाएँ महसूस करने की हमारी काबिलियत से। हर कोई इस व्याख्या से सहमत नहीं है, और शोध जारी है। कुछ वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि किसी अटपटे पल के बाद चेहरे की लाली दूसरों को शांत भी कर सकती है, जिससे छोटी-सी कहासुनी बड़े झगड़े में नहीं बदलती।

sec.t:
लगभग हर किसी का चेहरा कभी न कभी लाल होता है। पर कुछ लोगों के साथ यह बहुत ज़्यादा होता है और बहुत परेशान करता है। चेहरा लाल होने के तेज़ डर का एक नाम भी है: एरिथ्रोफ़ोबिया। अगर इससे तुम्हें घबराहट होती है या तुम इसकी वजह से कुछ करने से कतराते हो, तो किसी भरोसेमंद बड़े या डॉक्टर से बात करना अच्छा है। वे मदद कर सकते हैं।

अलग-अलग [[@skin-colour|रंग की त्वचा]] पर लाली अलग दिखती है। गहरी त्वचा पर लाल रंग कम नज़र आ सकता है, पर गर्माहट और एहसास बिल्कुल वैसे ही होते हैं।

लाल न होने की ज़ोर-ज़बरदस्ती से कोशिश आम तौर पर उल्टी पड़ती है। कुछ जानकार कहते हैं कि इसे होने दो और अपना काम करते रहो। और सबसे अजीब बात? किसी का चेहरा शर्म से लाल होते देखकर लोग अक्सर उसे और ज़्यादा पसंद करने लगते हैं। [[@kindness-science|छोटी-छोटी भलाइयाँ]] भी लोगों का दिल लगभग इसी तरह जीत लेती हैं।

text: तुम्हारा बिस्तर घरेलू धूल के कीटों का घर है। ये मकड़ियों के नन्हे रिश्तेदार हैं, लगभग चौथाई मिलीमीटर लंबे, इस वाक्य के आखिर में लगे पूर्णविराम से बड़े नहीं। इनकी आठ टाँगें होती हैं, आँखें नहीं होतीं और शरीर पारदर्शी होता है।

ये गद्दों, तकियों, कंबलों, सोफ़ों और कालीनों में रहते हैं। इनका पसंदीदा खाना वह मरी त्वचा है जो तुमसे हर समय झड़ती रहती है। बिस्तर इन्हें वह सब देता है जो ये चाहते हैं: खाना, गर्मी, और तुम्हारी साँस और पसीने से नमी। धरती के ज़्यादातर घरों में ये होते हैं, और ये न काटते हैं, न बीमारी फैलाते हैं।

sec.t:
तुम दिन भर त्वचा झाड़ते रहते हो, इतने नन्हे टुकड़ों में कि पता ही नहीं चलता। कुछ अनुमान कहते हैं कि हर मिनट दसियों हज़ार त्वचा कोशिकाएँ तुमसे झड़ जाती हैं। तुम ज़िंदगी का लगभग एक-तिहाई हिस्सा बिस्तर में बिताते हो, इसलिए उस त्वचा का बड़ा हिस्सा चादरों में पहुँच जाता है। पूरी कहानी [[@gross-skin-shedding|त्वचा कैसे झड़ती है]] में है।

धूल के कीट, बिस्तर में रहने वाली [[fungus|फफूँद]] की थोड़ी मदद से, इन टुकड़ों को तोड़कर खा जाते हैं। एक कीट कुछ महीने जीता है, और एक मादा दर्जनों अंडे दे सकती है। गर्म, नम घरों में इनकी गिनती तेज़ी से बढ़ती है।

ज़्यादातर लोगों के लिए धूल के कीट बेकसूर हैं। पर इनकी बीट में ऐसे प्रोटीन होते हैं जो [[@allergies|एलर्जी]] भड़का सकते हैं। जब तुम तकिया थपथपाते हो या बिस्तर ठीक करते हो, तो यह बीट हवा में उड़ती है और साँस के साथ अंदर चली जाती है।

जिन्हें एलर्जी है, उनके लिए इसका मतलब हो सकता है बंद या बहती नाक, छींकें, आँखों में खुजली, और कुछ लोगों में दमे का दौरा। धूल के कीट दुनिया में एलर्जी के सबसे आम [[allergen|कारणों]] में से एक हैं। डॉक्टर त्वचा पर एक छोटी-सी जाँच से पता लगा सकते हैं कि किसी को इनसे एलर्जी है या नहीं।

अगर तुम अक्सर छींकते हुए उठते हो, तो माँ-बाप या डॉक्टर को बताना अच्छा है। वे पता लगाने में मदद कर सकते हैं कि वजह धूल के कीट हैं या नहीं।

धूल के कीटों से पूरी तरह छुटकारा नहीं मिल सकता, पर इन्हें कम रखा जा सकता है। हर हफ़्ते चादरें और तकिए के गिलाफ़ लगभग 60 °C के गर्म पानी में धोने से ज़्यादातर मर जाते हैं। धूप और सूखी हवा भी मदद करती हैं। यह एक वजह है कि भारत में परिवार अक्सर गद्दे और रज़ाइयाँ छतों और बालकनियों पर धूप में डालते हैं।

खास गिलाफ़ गद्दों और तकियों को चारों ओर से ज़िप से बंद कर देते हैं, ताकि कीट अंदर रहें और बीट तुम्हारे चेहरे से दूर। बिस्तर पर कम खिलौने और घर में कम कालीन भी मदद करते हैं।

धूल के कीट उन बहुत-से छोटे जीवों में से बस एक हैं जो तुम्हारी ज़िंदगी में साझेदार हैं। तुम्हारी त्वचा पर भी अपने सूक्ष्म कीट रहते हैं, जिन्हें डेमोडेक्स कहते हैं। ये ज़्यादातर बड़ों की पलकों की जड़ों में और चेहरे पर रहते हैं, और रात में घूमने निकलते हैं। ये बैक्टीरिया और फफूँद की उस विशाल भीड़ में शामिल हैं जो हर किसी के शरीर पर रहती है, जिससे तुम [[@gross-body-bacteria|शरीर के कीटाणुओं]] वाली कहानी में मिल सकते हो।

text: Apps collect information about you, called data. Some of it you give on purpose, such as your name, age or photos. Much more is gathered quietly: where your phone is, what you tap, how long you watch a video and which other apps you use.

Apps use this data to work properly, to improve themselves and, very often, to show you [[@advertising|adverts]]. Free apps usually make money from ads, and ads that match your interests earn more. That's why your data is valuable. Laws in India and the US try to protect children's data in particular.

sec.t:
When you install an app, it may ask for permissions. These are switches that let it use parts of your phone, like the camera, microphone, contacts, photos or location. A map app needs your location. A photo editor needs your pictures. A game probably needs neither.

Location comes from your phone's [[@gps-how|GPS]], Wi-Fi and mobile towers. Some apps check it constantly, even when you aren't using them. Over a week, that can show where you live, which school you go to and where you play on Sundays. Photos can carry location too, and contacts reveal who your friends and family are, even if those people never installed the app.

In 1998 the United States passed COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. It says apps and websites aimed at children under 13 must get a parent's permission before collecting their personal data. That's why many apps say you must be 13 to join.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 goes further for young people. It says companies need a parent's consent to handle the data of anyone under 18. They are not supposed to track children's behaviour or aim ads at them. Europe has strict rules too. These laws take time to enforce, and not every company follows them well.

Since 2020, Apple's App Store has shown "privacy labels" that list what each app collects, a bit like the ingredients on a food packet. Google Play added a similar data safety section in 2022. They're worth a look before you download something new, though they rely on companies telling the truth.

You can also check permissions in your phone's settings and turn off anything an app doesn't need. Strong, different [[@passwords|passwords]] and two-step login make it harder for anyone to break into your accounts.

Before you sign up for something, ask an adult. Use a nickname instead of your full name where you can, and don't share your address, school or phone number in games or chats. Turn location off for apps that don't need it.

Remember that everything you post or search adds to your [[@digital-footprint|digital footprint]], which can last for years. Thinking before you tap is the simplest form of [[@privacy|privacy]]. Most companies aren't evil, but they are businesses, and your attention and data are what many of them sell.

text: Most phones and tablets use capacitive touchscreens. Just under [[@made-phone-screens|the glass]] is an invisible grid of very thin, see-through wires that carry a tiny electric charge, creating a weak electric field across the screen.

Your body conducts [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. When your fingertip comes close to the glass, it draws away a little of that charge at the spot you touch. A small chip constantly measures the grid. It notices exactly where the charge has changed and works out the position of your finger, many times every second.
That's why a gentle tap works, and why a pencil or a gloved finger usually does nothing.

sec.t:
The wires in a touchscreen must carry electricity yet let light through, so you can still see the picture beneath. They're often made of indium tin oxide, a material that conducts electricity but is almost transparent when spread very thin.

The wires run in rows and columns, like a cricket scoreboard grid. Where a row crosses a column, they form a tiny [[sensor|sensor]]. The chip checks each crossing over and over. When your finger is near one, that crossing's electrical reading changes, and the chip knows which row and which column you're touching.

Because every crossing is checked separately, the screen can track several fingers at once. That's how you pinch to zoom.

sec.h: Your body as part of the circuit
sec.t:
The trick relies on something called [[capacitance|capacitance]]: the ability to store a little electric charge. Your body, mostly salty water, is good at this. It's related to the effect behind [[@static-electricity|static electricity]], when you get a small shock from a door handle.

The [[@skin|skin]] on your fingertip lets this effect pass through easily. Thick wool or leather gloves keep your finger too far away and don't conduct, so the screen ignores you. Touchscreen gloves have conductive threads woven into their tips.

Water confuses the screen too. A few raindrops can conduct electricity and act like extra fingers, which is why wet phones sometimes tap things by themselves.

{{story:static-electricity}}

Before capacitive screens became common, many devices used resistive touchscreens. These have two flexible layers with a small gap between them. When you press, the top layer bends and touches the bottom one, completing a [[circuit|circuit]] at that spot.

Resistive screens work with any object, including a fingernail, a stylus or a gloved hand, but you have to press firmly. They were used on early handheld computers and still appear on some ticket machines, card machines and factory equipment. Some large screens instead use beams of invisible [[infrared|infrared]] light across their surface and sense where your finger breaks them.

In 1965, E.A. Johnson, an engineer at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, England, described a capacitive touchscreen for [[@air-traffic|air traffic controllers]]. It let them select planes on a radar screen with a finger.

In the early 1970s, engineers Frank Beck and Bent Stumpe at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva, built capacitive touchscreens to control a particle accelerator. CERN is also where the [[@web-invented|World Wide Web]] was invented.

Touchscreens spread to [[@atm-machines|ATMs]], ticket machines and handheld organisers. The iPhone in 2007 made multi-touch screens part of everyday life.

The touch layer is only part of the screen. Underneath, millions of tiny coloured dots called [[@pixels|pixels]] make the image. The phone matches where you touch with what's displayed at that spot, so tapping an icon opens the right app.

Some screens can now sense how hard you press, or notice your finger hovering just above the glass. Many phones vibrate briefly when you tap, so the flat glass feels a little like a real button.

text: Babylon was one of the great cities of the ancient world. It stood on the banks of the Euphrates river in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, in today's Iraq. People lived there for well over 2,000 years.

It rose to power twice. Around 1750 BCE, King [[@hammurabi|Hammurabi]] made it the capital of a large kingdom and set down his famous laws. More than a thousand years later, King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt it into a city of thick walls, glazed brick gates and a giant stepped temple tower. Its ruins lie about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad.

st.prompt: Babylonian mathematicians did their sums in a number system based on which number?
st.reveal: They counted in sixties, a system they took over from the Sumerians. Sixty can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, which made fractions easy. We still use it for minutes, seconds and degrees.

sec.t:
After centuries of being ruled by others, Babylon rose again in the 600s BCE. Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled from 605 to 562 BCE, filled it with building projects. The most famous was the Ishtar Gate, faced with bricks glazed a deep blue. On them marched rows of bulls and dragons in yellow and white. A long Processional Way, lined with glazed lions, led through it.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] from Germany dug up the gate between 1899 and 1917 and shipped many of the broken bricks to Berlin. There, the gate was pieced back together in a museum, where it towers over visitors today.

Most Babylonians were not kings or priests. They were farmers, brickmakers, weavers, boatmen and traders. Fields around the city were watered by canals dug from the Euphrates, and barley and dates were the main crops. Barley was so important that wages and loans were often counted in it.

Houses were built of mud brick around a small open courtyard, which kept rooms cool in the fierce summer heat. Children who trained as scribes went to a "tablet house", where they copied signs over and over on soft clay. Some of their practice tablets survive, mistakes and all. A few have the teacher's neat model on one side and the pupil's wobbly copy on the other.

In the middle of the city stood a ziggurat, a temple built like a stack of giant steps, called Etemenanki. It may have reached about 90 metres, as tall as a 30-storey building. Many historians think stories of it helped inspire the Bible's Tower of Babel.

Babylonian priests watched the sky every night and kept records for hundreds of years. Their star patterns fed into the [[zodiac|zodiac]] and the [[@constellations|constellations]] we still use.

Greek writers listed the Hanging Gardens of Babylon among the [[@seven-wonders|Seven Wonders]] of the ancient world. They described terraces of trees watered by machines lifting river water. Yet no clay tablet from Babylon mentions them, which is why experts still argue.

In 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great of [[@ancient-persia|Persia]] captured the city, mostly without a fight. Alexander the Great later planned to make it his capital and died in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in 323 BCE. After that the city slowly emptied. Its mud bricks crumbled back into mounds, and in 2019 the site was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text: मौलाना अबुल कलाम आज़ाद एक विद्वान, पत्रकार और स्वतंत्रता सेनानी थे, जो आज़ाद भारत के पहले शिक्षा मंत्री बने। उन्होंने अंग्रेज़ी राज के ख़िलाफ़ धारदार लेख लिखे, कुछ सबसे मुश्किल सालों में भारतीय राष्ट्रीय कांग्रेस की अगुवाई की, और अपनी ज़िंदगी के लगभग दस साल अंग्रेज़ों की जेलों में बिताए।

आज़ाद हिंदू-मुस्लिम एकता में पूरे दिल से विश्वास करते थे और भारत के [[@partition|बँटवारे]] के ख़िलाफ़ डटकर लड़े। आज़ादी के बाद उन्होंने दस साल से ज़्यादा समय देश के स्कूलों, विश्वविद्यालयों और कलाओं को आकार देने में लगाया। उनका जन्मदिन, 11 नवंबर, राष्ट्रीय शिक्षा दिवस के रूप में मनाया जाता है। "मौलाना" किसी विद्वान मुस्लिम आलिम के लिए इज़्ज़त से इस्तेमाल होने वाली उपाधि है।

बहुतों ने नहीं दिया। मौलाना आज़ाद बँटवारे के सबसे कड़े विरोधियों में थे। वे ऐसे एकजुट भारत के पक्ष में थे जहाँ हिंदू, मुसलमान और बाकी सब बराबर के नागरिक बनकर साथ रहें।

sec.t:
आज़ाद 1888 में मक्का में पैदा हुए, जहाँ उनके पिता, जो एक भारतीय धार्मिक विद्वान थे, उस समय रहते थे। जब वे छोटे ही थे, परिवार कलकत्ता, यानी आज के [[@kolkata|कोलकाता]], आ गया। वे किसी आम स्कूल में नहीं गए। उनके पिता और निजी शिक्षकों ने उन्हें अरबी, फ़ारसी, [[@urdu|उर्दू]], [[philosophy|दर्शनशास्त्र]] और गणित पढ़ाया, और अंग्रेज़ी उन्होंने ख़ुद पढ़-पढ़कर सीखी।

किशोर उम्र में ही वे पत्रिकाएँ लिखने और संपादित करने लगे। उन्होंने अपना तख़ल्लुस "आज़ाद" चुना, यानी स्वतंत्र, जो उनके आज़ाद ख़यालों से ख़ूब मेल खाता था।

1912 में, 23 साल की उम्र में, आज़ाद ने *अल-हिलाल* नाम का उर्दू साप्ताहिक शुरू किया। इसमें बड़ी-बड़ी सुर्ख़ियाँ और तस्वीरें होती थीं, जो उस ज़माने के उर्दू अख़बारों में कम ही दिखती थीं। यह भारतीय मुसलमानों से हिंदुओं के कंधे से कंधा मिलाकर आज़ादी के आंदोलन में उतरने की अपील करता था। इसकी बिक्री आसमान छूने लगी।

अंग्रेज़ों को यह रास नहीं आया। 1914 में उन्होंने इसका छापाख़ाना ज़ब्त कर लिया। आज़ाद ने दूसरा अख़बार निकाला, और 1916 में उन्हें बंगाल छोड़ने पर मजबूर किया गया और 1920 तक राँची में नज़रबंद रखा गया। बाहर आते ही वे गांधी के असहयोग आंदोलन में शामिल हो गए। 1923 में, 35 साल की उम्र में, वे कांग्रेस के अब तक के सबसे कम उम्र के अध्यक्ष बने।

आज़ादी पास आते-आते मुस्लिम लीग ने मुसलमानों के लिए अलग देश की माँग की। आज़ाद इससे बिल्कुल सहमत नहीं थे। उनका मानना था कि भारतीय मुसलमान भी उतने ही भारत के हैं जितना कोई और, और देश को बाँटने से सबको तकलीफ़ होगी।

1947 में भयानक हिंसा के बीच [[partition|बँटवारा]] हो ही गया। उसी साल अक्टूबर में आज़ाद दिल्ली की जामा मस्जिद में खड़े हुए और डरे हुए मुसलमानों से अपील की कि देश छोड़कर मत जाओ। उन्होंने कहा, भारत तुम्हारा घर है, यहीं रहो और इसे बनाने में हाथ बँटाओ। बहुत से लोग उस भाषण को उस दौर के सबसे दिल छू लेने वाले भाषणों में गिनते हैं।

1947 से 1958 में अपनी मौत तक शिक्षा मंत्री रहते हुए आज़ाद के सामने बहुत बड़ा काम था। ज़्यादातर भारतीय पढ़ नहीं सकते थे। उन्होंने बच्चों के लिए मुफ़्त और अनिवार्य शिक्षा पर ज़ोर दिया, और बड़ों की पढ़ाई पर भी।

उन्होंने ऐसी संस्थाएँ बनाने में भी मदद की जो आज भी बहुत मायने रखती हैं। पहला भारतीय प्रौद्योगिकी संस्थान, यानी IIT, 1951 में खड़गपुर में खुला। विश्वविद्यालयों की देखरेख करने वाला विश्वविद्यालय अनुदान आयोग उन्हीं के समय बना। साहित्य, संगीत और नृत्य, और दृश्य कलाओं की राष्ट्रीय अकादमियाँ भी। दुनिया भर की आज की [[@school-history|स्कूली]] व्यवस्थाओं की तरह उनकी योजना में भी विज्ञान और कला साथ-साथ चलते थे।

22 फ़रवरी 1958 को दिल्ली में आज़ाद का निधन हुआ। उन्हें जामा मस्जिद के पास दफ़नाया गया, जहाँ कभी उन्होंने वह भाषण दिया था। 1992 में उन्हें भारत रत्न दिया गया, जो भारत का सबसे बड़ा नागरिक सम्मान है। बताया जाता है कि जीते-जी उन्होंने इसे लेने से मना कर दिया था, क्योंकि उनका मानना था कि चुनने वाली समिति के लोगों को यह सम्मान नहीं मिलना चाहिए। 2008 से उनके जन्मदिन पर राष्ट्रीय शिक्षा दिवस मनाया जाता है, जो हर [[citizen|नागरिक]] तक पढ़ाई पहुँचाने के उनके सपने की याद दिलाता है।

text: The Non-Cooperation Movement was a huge, peaceful protest against British rule in India, led by [[@gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] from 1920 to 1922. Its idea was simple. The British ruled India with the help of Indians: as clerks, soldiers, lawyers, students and buyers of British goods. If Indians stopped cooperating, the government would struggle to work.

So people left government schools and colleges. Lawyers walked out of British courts. Some gave back medals and titles. Crowds lit bonfires of foreign cloth and began wearing homespun cotton instead. It was the first time the freedom movement reached so deeply into villages and small towns.

The Congress approved the plan at a special session in Calcutta in September 1920 and confirmed it at Nagpur that December. At Nagpur it also changed itself. Anyone could now join by paying four annas a year, and committees were set up in districts and villages, working in Indian languages as well as English.

st.prompt: In February 1922 Gandhi suddenly called off the Non-Cooperation Movement. Why?

options.t: A crowd set fire to a police station at Chauri Chaura and policemen died
The British agreed to give India self-rule
Gandhi became too ill to lead

st.reveal: At Chauri Chaura, in today's Uttar Pradesh, protesters attacked a police station after police fired on them, and 22 policemen were killed. Gandhi believed his movement had to stay non-violent, so he stopped it.
