National Archives of India, records of the freedom struggle.
n.certNote: The events are well documented. Historians and leaders of the time disagreed about whether Gandhi was right to call the movement off in 1922.

sec.t:
The years after the First World War left many Indians angry. More than a million Indians had served in the British war effort, and they expected more self-rule in return. Instead, in 1919, the Rowlatt Act let the police jail people without trial.

That April, British troops fired on a peaceful crowd at [[@jallianwala|Jallianwala Bagh]] in Amritsar, killing hundreds. At the same time, many Indian Muslims were upset that Britain was breaking up the Ottoman Empire, whose sultan many saw as the Khalifa, a religious leader. Their Khilafat movement joined with Gandhi's campaign, bringing Hindus and Muslims together in a way rarely seen before.

Gandhi promised swaraj, self-rule, within a year if people stuck together. Thousands of students left British-run colleges. New national schools opened, including Jamia Millia Islamia and Gujarat Vidyapith, both founded in 1920 and still running.

Famous lawyers, including Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das, gave up rich careers. Women joined in large numbers, picketing shops that sold foreign cloth and liquor. When Britain's Prince of Wales toured India in late 1921, many cities greeted him with closed shops and empty streets. Spinning wheels hummed in homes, and wearing [[@khadi|khadi]], handspun cloth, became a badge of protest.

Gandhi himself handed back the Kaisar-i-Hind medal the British had given him for running an ambulance corps in South Africa. Rabindranath Tagore had already given up his knighthood in 1919, after Jallianwala Bagh. Even so, Tagore had doubts about parts of the movement, such as students leaving school, and he and Gandhi argued about it in public, politely but firmly.

{{story:khadi}}

On 4 February 1922, in the small town of Chauri Chaura in today's Uttar Pradesh, police fired on protesters. The angry crowd set fire to the police station, and 22 policemen died.

Gandhi was horrified. He believed that freedom won by violence would lead to more violence. A week later he called off the whole movement. Many leaders were shocked, including Motilal Nehru and the young Subhas Chandra Bose, who felt the movement was close to success. Soon after, Gandhi was arrested and sentenced to six years in prison, though he was released after two.

The British did not leave in 1922, and the promise of swaraj in a year was not met. The Hindu-Muslim unity of those years also faded after the Khilafat cause ended.

Still, the movement turned the Congress from a party of educated leaders into a mass movement of farmers, workers, students and women. It made boycott and homespun cloth familiar tools, building on the earlier [[@swadeshi|Swadeshi]] movement. Eight years later, ordinary Indians would use the same methods when they followed Gandhi on the Salt March.

text: Roman roads were straight mainly because a straight line is the shortest way between two places, and Rome needed to move soldiers fast. A legion marching on a straight road reached trouble sooner, and supply carts followed more easily.

Straight lines were also easier to survey. Roman engineers sighted from one high point to the next using simple tools, laying out long straight sections between them. Where a hill or river got in the way, they changed direction and set off straight again. So a Roman road is often a series of straight lines joined by bends.

st.prompt: A Roman mile was "mille passus". A thousand of what?

options.t: Paces, where one pace was two steps

st.reveal: A Roman pace (passus) counted two steps, left and right, about 1.48 m. So a thousand paces came to about 1.48 km. Our word "mile" comes from "mille", the Latin for a thousand.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Roman road system; Appian Way.
British Museum, Roman Britain collection.
Chevallier R. (1976) Roman Roads. Batsford.

They were straight where the land allowed. Around steep hills, rivers and marshes, Roman engineers curved and zigzagged their roads like anyone else.

sec.t:
The most famous Roman road is the Via Appia, or Appian Way. It was begun in 312 BCE by an official named Appius Claudius, who gave it his name. It ran south from Rome to Capua and was later extended to Brindisi, on the heel of Italy, about 560 km in all. Romans called it the "queen of long roads".

Parts of it can still be walked today, with the original grey paving stones worn smooth by carts and feet. Tombs and monuments line its edges, because Romans were not allowed to bury their dead inside the city.

Roman surveyors used a tool called a groma. It was a wooden cross on a pole, with a weighted string hanging from each arm. When the strings hung straight down, the cross was level. By lining up the strings with markers far away, a surveyor could set out long straight lines and right angles.

Signal fires or smoke on hilltops may also have helped teams line up stretches many kilometres long. In England, a road called the Fosse Way runs for about 370 km. Along nearly 300 km of it, from Lincoln to Ilchester, it is never more than about 10 km from a straight line.

Along major roads stood stone pillars called milestones, one every Roman mile. They showed the distance to the next town or to Rome, and the name of the emperor who built or repaired the road. In Rome's forum stood a golden milestone, which is part of why people said that all roads lead to Rome.

Official messengers changed horses at stations along the way, and could carry news across the [[empire|empire]] in days rather than weeks. Traders, pilgrims and ordinary travellers used the roads too, spreading goods and ideas.

India had great roads too. The Uttarapatha, an ancient route across the north, linked the Gangetic plains to the north-west. Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] wrote that he had planted [[@banyan|banyan trees]] for shade and dug wells along roads for travellers and animals. In the 1500s, Sher Shah Suri rebuilt a long highway with rest houses, which later became part of the Grand Trunk Road, running from Bengal towards the north-west.

Many modern roads in Europe follow Roman routes, because the Romans had already chosen the best line. The [[@ancient-rome|Roman Empire]] fell long ago, but its road network shaped where towns grew and how people still travel. In Italy, some main roads still carry the names of the Roman roads they follow, such as the Via Appia and the Via Flaminia.

text: At the top of the Eiffel Tower, you stand on a small, windy platform about 276 metres above Paris. The city spreads out below like a map. You can follow the River Seine as it curves past bridges and spot the white domes of Sacré-Cœur on its hill. On a clear day you can see for tens of kilometres. Below, the boats on the river look like toys and the trees of the Champ de Mars park form neat green rows.

Getting there takes two lifts. The first climbs one of the tower's four slanting legs to the second floor. A second lift goes straight up the narrow middle to the top. The ride is short but stomach-turning, with iron beams flashing past the glass. Up top, part of the deck is enclosed by windows, and part is open to the wind behind a safety mesh.

st.prompt: On a hot summer day, the top of the Eiffel Tower can be several centimetres higher than in winter. Why?

options.t: Its iron expands in the heat
Its legs sink less into dry ground
Crowds push down less in summer

st.reveal: Metal swells slightly when it warms. Over 300 metres of iron, that adds up to several centimetres. The sunny side can also expand more than the shady side, so the top leans very slightly away from the sun.

d.try: Look at a ruler-straight metal railing or gate on a hot afternoon and again on a cool morning. You won't see the change, but builders leave small gaps in bridges and rail tracks for exactly this reason. Look for those gaps on a bridge or a flyover when you cross one with an adult.
myth: Parisians loved the Eiffel Tower from the start.

sec.t:
Visitors who prefer stairs can walk up 674 steps to the second floor, about 115 m up. Many families take the stairs to the first floor, where a section of glass floor lets you look straight down at people the size of ants, 57 m below.

The ride to the top uses [[@elevators|lifts]] designed for an unusual problem. The tower's legs are curved, so the lower lifts must travel along a slope that changes angle as they rise. Engineers in 1889 had to invent new ways to do it, and the lifts have been rebuilt several times since.

The full climb from the ground to the top is about 1,665 steps, but the stairs above the second floor are closed to the public. Hungry visitors can stop at restaurants on the first and second floors. At the very top there is a small champagne bar, probably the highest place to buy a drink in Paris.

{{story:elevators}}

Gustave Eiffel, whose company built the [[@eiffel-tower|tower]], kept a small apartment near the top. He used it for scientific experiments on weather and air resistance, and for entertaining important guests. In 1889, the American inventor Thomas Edison visited and gave Eiffel one of his new phonographs.

Today the room is open to view through windows. Wax figures of Eiffel, Edison and Eiffel's daughter sit inside, as if chatting in their Sunday best. Eiffel's company also designed the iron skeleton inside the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]] in New York.

The tower went up in just over two years, built from about 18,000 iron parts held together by roughly 2.5 million rivets. It sways only slightly in strong winds, usually by a few centimetres, because its open lattice of iron lets the air pass through. Heat has more effect. On hot days, the iron expands and the tower grows by several centimetres.

Keeping it from rusting is a never-ending job. About every seven years, painters cover all 18,000 iron parts by hand, using around 60 tonnes of paint. The latest repainting, begun in 2019, brought back a yellow-brown that Gustave Eiffel chose in 1907. It is darker at the bottom and lighter at the top, so it looks even against the sky.

When it opened for the World's Fair in 1889, the tower was the tallest structure in the world, until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930. Many people in [[@paris|Paris]] first hated it. It survived partly because it was useful for radio, and antennas still stand on top.

Every evening after dark, the tower glitters for five minutes at the start of each hour, as 20,000 small lights flash at random. At the 2024 Paris Olympics, each medal held a small piece of iron taken from the tower during repairs, so athletes carried a little bit of it home.

text: Majuli is an island in the middle of the Brahmaputra River in Assam, in northeast India. In 2016, Guinness World Records recognised it as the largest river island in the world, and that is the title most people know.

But the answer is not so simple. Bananal Island in Brazil is much bigger, and it too sits between rivers. Experts argue over whether it counts as a true river island. Meanwhile, Majuli itself keeps shrinking, because the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] eats away at its edges every [[monsoon|monsoon]].

st.prompt: Majuli sits in the middle of a huge river. What is slowly happening to its size?

options.t: It is shrinking, because the river washes away its banks
It is growing every year as new land rises up
It stays exactly the same, because it is solid rock

st.reveal: Majuli is made of soft silt and sand, not rock. Every monsoon, the Brahmaputra floods and washes away parts of its banks. The river also drops new sand in other places, but for the last century the island has lost far more than it has gained.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Majuli and Bananal Island entries.

n.certNote: Guinness World Records named Majuli the largest river island in 2016, but Bananal Island in Brazil is far bigger and is also surrounded by rivers. The answer depends on how you define a river island, and Majuli's own size changes every year as the river eats and builds land.

Guinness World Records gave Majuli that title in 2016, but Bananal Island in Brazil, between two rivers, covers about 19,000 km², many times more than Majuli. Some experts don't count Bananal because of how its rivers split and join, so the record depends on the definition.

sec.t:
Majuli is not made of rock. It is a giant bank of [[sediment|sediment]]: sand and silt carried down from the Himalayas and dropped by the river. The Brahmaputra is one of the widest rivers in the world in flood, and in places it spreads into many channels around the island.

Soft land like this is easy to wash away. Records suggest that in the early 1900s Majuli covered about 1,250 square kilometres. Today it is much smaller, though measurements differ because the banks shift every year. A big earthquake in 1950 changed the river's flow and is thought to have made the [[@floods-why|floods]] and [[erosion|erosion]] worse.

In the 1500s, the saint and reformer Srimanta Sankardev visited Majuli. He spread a form of Hindu devotion to Krishna that used music, drama and dance. His followers built [[monastery|monasteries]] called satras on the island, and some of them still stand.

The satras are famous for Sattriya dance and for mask-making. At Samaguri Satra, craftsmen shape huge [[@indian-theatre|masks]] of demons and gods from bamboo, clay and cloth for plays about the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Some masks are so big that they cover the actor's whole body.

So is Majuli the biggest? Bananal Island in Brazil sits between the Araguaia and Javaés rivers and covers about 19,000 square kilometres, an area bigger than the whole of Majuli many times over. Britannica describes Bananal as one of the largest river islands in the world.

Guinness looked at it differently and named Majuli the record holder in 2016. Part of the argument is about what counts. Is an island formed where a river splits and rejoins the same as one built up in the middle of a single wide river? Geographers don't fully agree, so both claims appear in books.

Assam's government and the Brahmaputra Board have built embankments, dropped sandbags and planted grass and trees along the banks to slow the erosion. Some stretches have held. Others have been swept away in a single bad flood. A road bridge linking Majuli to the mainland has been planned, which would change daily life for islanders who now depend on ferries.

Each winter, Majuli's [[@wetlands|wetlands]] fill with [[migration|migrating]] birds, including ducks and geese that fly in from colder lands to the north. Visitors come for the birds, the satras and the quiet. Whether or not it holds the world record, there is no other place quite like it.

text: J.R.R. Tolkien was an English professor and writer, best known for *The Hobbit* (1937) and *The Lord of the Rings* (1954–1955). These books created Middle-earth, a world of hobbits, elves, dwarves, wizards and dragons, and helped shape [[@fantasy-books|modern fantasy writing]].

His day job was the study of old languages. He taught Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons, at Oxford University for decades. He loved inventing languages so much that he built whole histories and maps around them. *The Lord of the Rings* has sold well over a hundred million copies and been turned into famous films.

sec.t:
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was born in 1892 in Bloemfontein, [[@south-africa|South Africa]], where his father worked for a bank. He moved to England with his mother when he was three. His father died soon afterwards, and his mother died when he was twelve. A Catholic priest became his guardian.

As a boy he was already inventing languages. At Oxford he studied old tongues such as Old English, Old Norse and Gothic, and fell in love with Finnish and Welsh. His two main Elvish languages, Quenya and Sindarin, borrow the sound of Finnish and Welsh.

In 1916 he fought in the Battle of the Somme in the [[@world-war-one|First World War]]. Most of his close school friends were killed in the war. He fell ill with trench fever and was sent home. Some readers see the dead marshes and ruined lands of Mordor as echoes of the trenches, though Tolkien warned against reading his book as a simple copy of real events.

{{story:world-war-one}}

After the war, Tolkien worked on the Oxford English Dictionary, researching the history of words beginning with W, such as "wasp", "walrus" and "warm". It suited him perfectly. To Tolkien, every word had a story.

He also studied old poems such as *Beowulf*, in which a hero fights a dragon, and the Norse sagas. Their dragons, dwarves and rings found their way into his own stories. Even the names of the dwarves in *The Hobbit*, such as Thorin, Bombur and Fili, come from a list in an old Norse poem. So does the name of the wizard, Gandalf.

sec.h: From a blank page to Middle-earth
sec.t:
Tolkien told the story of the blank exam page in a letter. He made up *The Hobbit* for his own children, then published it in 1937. It was a success, and the publisher asked for a sequel.

That sequel took him about twelve years. *The Lord of the Rings* follows the hobbit Frodo on a journey to destroy a ring of terrible power. It is far darker and longer than *The Hobbit*. Tolkien read chapters aloud to a group of friends who met in Oxford pubs, called the Inklings. One of them was [[@cs-lewis|C. S. Lewis]], who encouraged him to keep going.

Between 2001 and 2003, the director Peter Jackson released three films of *The Lord of the Rings*, shot in [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]]. The last one, *The Return of the King*, won 11 Oscars, tying the record. Hobbiton, the village set, is now visited by tourists from around the world.

Tolkien's languages are now studied by fans who write poems in Elvish. That would surely have pleased the professor who once said he wrote his stories to give his languages a home.

text: इंडो-चाइनीज़ खाना उन चीनी परिवारों ने बनाया जो भारत में, ज़्यादातर कोलकाता में, आकर बस गए और भारतीय ग्राहकों के लिए खाना पकाने लगे। दशकों तक वे अपने नुस्ख़ों में बदलाव करते रहे। उन्होंने हरी मिर्च, [[@ginger-garlic|लहसुन, अदरक]], धनिया और ख़ूब सारे मसाले डालने शुरू किए। नतीजा एक बिल्कुल अपना अलग खाना निकला, जो चीन के खाने से काफ़ी अलग है।

इसके मशहूर पकवानों में चिली चिकन, हक्का नूडल्स, फ़्राइड राइस, स्वीट कॉर्न सूप, अमेरिकन चॉप्सी और हर तरह का मंचूरियन शामिल है। आज यह हर जगह मिलता है, [[@food-trucks|कॉलेज के गेट पर खड़े ठेले]] से लेकर बड़े रेस्तराँ तक। बहुत-से भारतीयों के लिए यह मन को सुकून देने वाला खाना है, और कुछ ने तो चीन का असली खाना कभी चखा ही नहीं।

sec.t:
कोलकाता के [[@restaurants-history|शुरुआती चीनी रेस्तराँ]] लगभग वैसा ही खाना परोसते थे जैसा कैंटोनीज़ परिवार घर पर खाते थे। पर भारतीय ग्राहकों को ज़्यादा तीखा और ज़्यादा चटपटा चाहिए था। रसोइए लहसुन और अदरक के साथ मिर्च तलने लगे, सोयाबीन में [[fermentation|ख़मीर उठाकर]] बनने वाली सोया सॉस ज़्यादा डालने लगे, और ग्रेवी को [[@non-newtonian|कॉर्नफ़्लोर]] से गाढ़ा करने लगे, ताकि वह हर टुकड़े से लिपट जाए।

धीरे-धीरे पकवान अपनी जड़ों से दूर होते गए। भारत के हक्का नूडल्स सब्ज़ियों, सिरके और चिली सॉस के साथ तेज़ आँच पर भूने जाते हैं। "शेज़वान" सॉस का नाम चीन के सिचुआन प्रांत पर पड़ा है, पर भारतीय शेज़वान लाल मिर्च और लहसुन का तीखा पेस्ट है। उसमें असली सिचुआन काली मिर्च नहीं होती, जो जीभ को सुन्न कर देती है।

सबसे मशहूर कहानी नेल्सन वांग की है। वे कोलकाता में चीनी माता-पिता के घर पैदा हुए थे। बाद में वे मुंबई चले गए और क्रिकेट क्लब ऑफ़ इंडिया में खाना पकाने लगे। उन्होंने बताया कि 1975 में एक ग्राहक ने कुछ ऐसा माँगा जो मेन्यू में न हो। तो उन्होंने चिकन के टुकड़ों को कॉर्नफ़्लोर के घोल में तल लिया। फिर उन्हें लहसुन, अदरक, हरी मिर्च और सोया की ग्रेवी में उछाला, ठीक वैसे जैसे कोई भारतीय रसोइया मसाला भूनना शुरू करता है।

उन्होंने इसका नाम रखा चिकन मंचूरियन। जल्दी ही गोभी और दूसरी सब्ज़ियों वाले शाकाहारी रूप भी आ गए और पूरे देश में फैल गए। बाद में वांग ने मुंबई में चाइना गार्डन नाम का एक मशहूर रेस्तराँ खोला।

1962 में भारत और चीन के बीच युद्ध के दौरान भारतीय चीनियों को बहुत तकलीफ़ झेलनी पड़ी, जबकि उनमें से ज़्यादातर भारत में ही पैदा हुए थे। बहुतों को राजस्थान के देवली में एक कैंप में भेज दिया गया, और कुछ को देश छोड़ने पर मजबूर किया गया। दूसरे लोग बाद में कनाडा, ऑस्ट्रेलिया और अमेरिका चले गए।

कोलकाता का चीनी समुदाय अब पहले से काफ़ी छोटा है, पर पुराने बाशिंदों के [[descendant|वंशज]] आज भी यहाँ रहते हैं। और रविवार की सुबह टेरेटी बाज़ार के पास ठेलों पर भाप में पके बन, [[@food-momos|मोमो जैसे डंपलिंग]] और फ़िश-बॉल सूप बिकते हैं। यह [[@breakfast-world|पीढ़ियों से चला आ रहा नाश्ता]] है।

इंडो-चाइनीज़ खाना काफ़ी कुछ अमेरिका के [[@tex-mex|टेक्स-मेक्स]] जैसा है। दोनों तब बने जब एक देश के रसोइयों ने दूसरे देश के लोगों को खाना खिलाया। अब यह [[@indian-diaspora|विदेश में बसे भारतीयों]] के साथ दुनिया घूम रहा है। न्यू जर्सी, टोरंटो और लंदन के रेस्तराँ चिली पनीर और गोभी मंचूरियन परोसते हैं, और हर तरह के लोग इन्हें मँगाते हैं।

text: Food is frozen by pulling heat out of it until the water inside turns to ice. At −18 °C, the usual temperature of a home freezer, [[bacteria|bacteria]] and moulds can't grow, and the chemical changes that make food go bad slow almost to a stop.

The real trick is speed. Freeze food slowly and it can turn mushy when it thaws. Freeze it very fast, in minutes rather than hours, and it comes out tasting much closer to fresh. Factories use blasts of freezing air, ice-cold metal plates or even liquid nitrogen to freeze food as quickly as possible.

st.prompt: Why does food frozen very fast taste better than food frozen slowly?

options.t: Fast freezing makes smaller ice crystals that do less damage
Slow freezing lets the flavour escape as steam

st.reveal: When food freezes slowly, water forms large, spiky ice crystals that tear the walls of the food's cells. When it thaws, juice leaks out and the food goes mushy. Fast freezing makes tiny crystals that leave the cells mostly whole.

sec.t:
Between about 1912 and 1915, an American naturalist named Clarence Birdseye lived in Labrador, in the far northeast of Canada. In winter the air there could drop to −40 °C. He watched Inuit fishers catch fish through holes in the ice. The fish froze almost instantly in the bitter wind.

Months later, when the fish were cooked, they tasted fresh. Birdseye wondered why, since frozen food sold in American cities at that time was usually soggy and bland. He decided the answer was the speed of freezing, and set out to copy the [[@arctic|Arctic]] with machines.

Today, peas, corn and chopped vegetables are usually washed and dipped briefly in boiling water first. This step, called blanching, stops natural [[enzyme|enzymes]] that would otherwise slowly change their colour and taste even in the freezer. Then they travel on a conveyor through a tunnel of air at around −30 °C or colder, which freezes each piece separately.

Some foods, such as prawns or [[@berries|berries]], are frozen in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C. That is so cold that it freezes them almost instantly. Ice cream is frozen while being stirred, so that the crystals stay tiny and the result is smooth, which is the secret of good [[@ice-cream|ice cream]].

Frozen food has to stay frozen all the way from the factory to your kitchen. Refrigerated lorries, cold stores and shop freezers make up a "cold chain". If any link breaks and the food thaws and refreezes, its quality drops.

India grows huge amounts of fruit, vegetables and fish, but much of it spoils before it is eaten because there are not enough cold stores and refrigerated trucks, especially near farms. Better cold chains could cut [[@food-waste|food waste]] a lot. In the USA, most families have a large freezer at home, and frozen [[@pizza|pizza]], vegetables and waffles are everyday food.

sec.h: Is frozen food good for you?
sec.t: Freezing does not add anything to food. It simply pauses it. A bag of plain frozen peas or spinach can be just as nutritious as fresh. Ready-made frozen meals are a different story, because some contain a lot of salt, sugar or fat, so it is worth reading the label. In Indian supermarkets you can now find frozen parathas, momos and sweetcorn, which shows how far Birdseye's idea from a frozen Canadian lake has travelled.
